As at 23 November 2026 the following are NOT law: the 35p mileage rate above 10,000 miles from 6 April 2027; the £3,000 trading allowance from 2027-28; the 50% main-rate FYA from 1 January 2027 and 12% WDA from 6 April 2027; 24/44/49% savings and property rates for 2027-28; the BADR lifetime limit cut to £500,000; More Timely Payments from April 2029; the extension of points-based penalties to all SA filers from April 2027; and the 4%/4% late payment penalty rates for 2027-28. Guidance is HMRC's view, not law (Gunnarsson [2025] UKUT 247 (TCC)): always check the statute. Rates and thresholds here are UK-wide or for England, Wales and Northern Ireland; Scottish income tax rates differ.

cases.name: Mallalieu v Drummond (Inspector of Taxes)
cases.principle: Whether spending is exclusively for the trade depends on the trader's object at the time, which a tribunal may infer beyond their conscious motive. A barrister's plain court clothes also met her ordinary need for warmth and decency, so the dual purpose barred any deduction; a purely incidental effect, as opposed to a purpose, would not.
cases.relevance: Plain show blacks, smart clothes for corporate events and boots or jackets that are part of an everyday wardrobe are not deductible, even if worn only at work. Genuine PPE (steel-toe boots, gloves, hi-vis, harnesses), uniforms and costumes are (BIM37910). The object-versus-effect distinction supports claims where a private benefit is merely incidental.
cases.status: Good law and the leading authority on dual purpose; not overruled. The statute it construed (ICTA 1970 s130(a)) is now ITTOIA 2005 s34(1)(a), with s34(2) apportionment. Applied in Interfish [2014] EWCA Civ 876 and Samadian [2014] UKUT 13 (TCC).

cases.name: MacKinlay (Inspector of Taxes) v Arthur Young McClelland Moores & Co
cases.principle: Removal expenses paid to partners asked to relocate for the firm were not deductible, because the spending inevitably also served their private purpose of setting up a family home. Some results are so inextricably part of an activity that they count as a purpose of it, whatever the payer says was intended.
cases.relevance: Personal relocation costs, or the costs of a second home near a long-running client, are not deductible for a sole trader. Spending that inherently delivers a private benefit (a home, food, ordinary clothing) fails s34 however strong the business reason.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Bentleys, Stokes and Lowless v Beeson (Inspector of Taxes)
cases.principle: 'Wholly' refers to the amount and 'exclusively' to the purpose, and the business purpose must be the sole purpose. Spending whose sole object is business is not disqualified merely because the activity necessarily brings some other result with it.
cases.relevance: An inherent side-benefit (a pleasant hotel near the venue, enjoyable travel) does not defeat a deduction if the trip's only object is business; an independent private object, however small, does. Its result on client entertaining is now reversed by the s45 entertainment bar.
cases.status: Good law on the sole-purpose principle; the result on entertaining is superseded by statute (ITTOIA 2005 s45 / CTA 2009 s1298).
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's Business Income Manual summary of the case (BIM37400), not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Strong & Co of Romsey Ltd v Woodifield (Surveyor of Taxes)
cases.principle: Damages paid by a brewer-innkeeper to a guest injured by a falling chimney were not deductible: the loss fell on it as householder rather than as trader, and a deduction needs a disbursement made for the purpose of earning the profits, not one merely connected with the trade.
cases.relevance: A purpose and 'losses not connected with the trade' case (ITTOIA s34(1)(b)), not a capital case. In practice HMRC allows civil damages arising from day-to-day trading (for example accidental damage to a venue's or client's kit) but not penalties for breaking the law (BIM38510, BIM37300).
cases.status: Good law (not overruled) but narrowly applied. HMRC BIM37300 says the 'capacity' test it started is of doubtful utility (citing Harrods (Buenos Aires) Ltd v Taylor-Gooby (1964) 41 TC 450), and BIM38510 tells officers to allow civil damages from day-to-day trading. The rules are now in ITTOIA 2005 s34(1)(a)-(b).

cases.name: Atherton (HM Inspector of Taxes) v British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd
cases.principle: A lump sum to start a staff pension fund was capital. Spending made once and for all to bring into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade is, absent special circumstances, capital rather than revenue.
cases.relevance: The 'enduring benefit' test is the starting point for capital v revenue: durable kit, a vehicle or a long-term right, as against repairs, consumables and hire. On the cash basis it matters less for equipment (s33A) but still matters for cars, training, land and intangibles.
cases.status: Good law (the general test), refined by later cases; the specific pension outcome is superseded by statute.

cases.name: Tucker (Inspector of Taxes) v Granada Motorway Services Ltd
cases.principle: A one-off payment to a landlord to change the rent formula was capital, because it was spent on the lease (an identifiable capital asset, even though unassignable and with no balance-sheet value) to make it more advantageous. As a starting point, spending to acquire, dispose of or improve a fixed asset is capital; spending to maintain it may be revenue.
cases.relevance: Upgrading or modifying kit, a vehicle, or a long-term contract or lease is capital; restoring it to working order (repairs, servicing) is revenue. Matters on the accruals basis and for cars on the cash basis.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in BIM35320, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Lawson (Inspector of Taxes) v Johnson Matthey plc
cases.principle: A £50m payment into a collapsing banking subsidiary, required before the Bank of England would take its worthless shares for £1, was revenue: in substance it saved the company's own trade and created no asset or lasting advantage. Wanting to preserve the trade does not by itself make a payment revenue; the test is what the payment was really for, and a once-and-for-all payment can be revenue.
cases.relevance: A one-off or large payment is not automatically capital. A payment to remove an obstacle to continued trading can be revenue unless linked to acquiring, disposing of or improving a capital asset; a counterweight when HMRC labels an unusual payment capital.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Caillebotte (Inspector of Taxes) v Quinn
cases.principle: A self-employed carpenter working at sites near home could not deduct any part of his lunches, not even the extra cost of eating away from home: a person must eat in order to live, not in order to work, and trying to apportion exposes the duality. Protective clothing differs because warmth and decency are incidental to the protection the trade needs.
cases.relevance: Day-to-day meals at local or regular venues, and the extra cost of eating on site, are not deductible. Meals become deductible only under ITTOIA s57A (itinerant trade or occasional journeys outside the normal pattern) or with a business overnight stay (BIM37670, BIM37675).
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in BIM37660, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Horton v Young (Inspector of Taxes)
cases.principle: A self-employed bricklayer with no business premises, who agreed contracts, kept tools and did his books at home, could deduct travel between home and a series of temporary sites, because home was the base from which the trade radiated. At first instance Brightman J said home-to-site travel for a trade itinerant by nature is normally wholly and exclusively for the trade, however long each job lasts.
cases.relevance: Central to a touring technician: travel from a home base to varying venues (mileage, fuel, trains, flights) is deductible. A long single-venue engagement, regular predictable workplaces, or a home far outside the working area can lose this protection (Samadian; BIM37620, BIM37675).
cases.status: Good law (not overruled), but narrowed in application by Samadian [2014] UKUT 13 (TCC) and distinguished in Hamish Taylor [2020] UKFTT 416 (TC).
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in BIM37620, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Dr Samad Samadian v HMRC
cases.citation: [2014] UKUT 13 (TCC); appeal no. FTC/53/2013 (on appeal from [2013] UKFTT 115 (TC))
cases.court: Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber), Sales J
cases.principle: Travel between home (even a home with a genuine office) and a place of business attended on a regular, predictable pattern is not deductible, because part of its purpose is to live away from the work; travel for genuinely itinerant work, and between two places of business purely for business, is deductible. Horton v Young covers only the narrow case where home is the only place of business and the work locations are unpredictable.
cases.relevance: One-off venues for short engagements arranged from home are itinerant work. A venue, warehouse, rehearsal studio or production office attended regularly becomes a place of business, and home-to-there journeys stop being deductible even with a home office (FTT [83], approved at UT [22]). Travel from a PAYE job to freelance work is not deductible ([40]); a special trip home to fetch something needed for the job is ([27]); a stop to do employment duties, or (obiter) a meal with a friend, can taint a journey. Sales J lists the categories at [46].
cases.status: Good law. Not overruled; Find Case Law shows no further appeal. ITTOIA 2005 s34 is unchanged. HMRC's BIM37600-37635 (updated 4 August 2026) do not cite it by name but reach the same results via Newsom v Robertson, Horton v Young and Jackman v Powell.

cases.name: Interfish Ltd v HMRC
cases.principle: Where the tribunal finds two purposes, one not the trade's (supporting a struggling rugby club as well as winning goodwill), the payment fails; there is no rule that an intermediate purpose pursued on the way to an ultimate business aim can be disregarded.
cases.relevance: Sponsorship of, donations to, or discounted work for a friend's production or a local club fail if part of the aim is to help them, even if goodwill also follows. Do not accept 'it was ultimately for business' where a second purpose exists.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: McKnight (Inspector of Taxes) v Sheppard
cases.principle: Fines and penalties for breaking the law or regulatory rules are not deductible, but legal costs of defending disciplinary proceedings that threatened the trade were, because the trader's purpose was to preserve the trade and any benefit to his reputation was an effect, not a purpose.
cases.relevance: Parking PCNs, speeding fines, congestion and ULEZ penalties, and HMRC late-filing or late-payment penalties are never deductible. Legal or professional fees defending the business (for example a contract dispute with a production company) can be.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: ScottishPower (SCPL) Ltd and others v HMRC
cases.principle: Redress payments of about £28m made to consumers under Ofgem settlements, in substance to avoid substantial penalties, were not deductible: payments of a penal character, including those agreed instead of a fine, are not incurred for the purposes of the trade (CTA 2009 s54(1)(a), the equivalent of ITTOIA s34). The bar comes from construing the statute, and substance prevails over labels such as 'voluntary'.
cases.relevance: The latest top-court statement on the purpose test. Never present fines, penalties, or settlements in place of them as allowable, even if called voluntary or paid to a third party. Interest on late tax is separately disallowed by ITTOIA s54.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Dass v Special Commissioner and others
cases.principle: Fees for a course leading to a new qualification that would let the trader move into a new area of practice were capital under the Atherton enduring-benefit test; a refresher course that updates or hones existing expertise is revenue.
cases.relevance: Training that updates or adds skills in the existing field is deductible: IPAF or PASMA renewals, rigging or safety refreshers, training on a new lighting or sound console. A course to enter a new profession is capital and also barred on the cash basis by s33A. HMRC's BIM35660 has worked examples.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: HMRC v Tim Healy
cases.court: Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber), Judges Timothy Herrington and John Clark
cases.principle: Accommodation costs are not automatically excluded: they are deductible if the only purpose is business and warmth and shelter are merely incidental, but not if meeting personal needs is a shared purpose. There is no fixed time limit; the longer the stay, the more likely a private purpose, and the tribunal must find whether the trader saw the engagement as temporary. Nine guiding principles are set out at [66].
cases.relevance: Governs hotels, digs and short lets for tours, runs and long engagements away from home. A long engagement does not by itself defeat a claim ([80], [82]). Evidence that matters: the contract term, a break clause matching the engagement, going home at weekends, not moving belongings in, and accommodation taken only because of a specific distant job ([79]-[83]). Principle (2) at [66]: hotels on business trips and accommodation for an itinerant trader can be wholly for business.
cases.status: Good law (UT decision, not overruled). It remitted the case; on rehearing the FTT disallowed the rent for dual purpose ([2015] UKFTT 233 (TC)).

cases.name: Tim Healy v HMRC (rehearing after remittal)
cases.court: First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), Judge Christopher Staker
cases.principle: An actor's three-bedroom London flat rented for a West End run was not deductible because he chose it partly so that visiting family and friends could stay; that independent private purpose made the cost dual-purpose, no identifiable proportion under s34(2) was proved, and it made no difference that it cost no more than a hotel ([36]-[41]).
cases.relevance: When working away, do not choose bigger accommodation to host a partner, family or friends, and do not have them stay: a private purpose can taint the whole cost, and the burden of proving a business proportion is on the trader. The earlier FTT decision ([2012] UKFTT 246 (TC)) also refused subsistence (£4,094) and taxi (£4,080) claims for the run; those refusals were not appealed.
cases.status: Good law as an FTT decision (binds no one); it applies the binding UT principles in HMRC v Healy [2013] UKUT 337 (TCC).
cases.note: The tribunal database lists only the 2012 and 2015 FTT decisions; Upper Tribunal and Court of Appeal records were not fully checked for any further appeal.

cases.name: Hamish Taylor v HMRC
cases.court: First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), Judge John Manuell and Mrs Jane Shillaker
cases.principle: A subcontractor who lived in Melrose but stayed 165 nights in a Swindon hotel, working a variety of subcontracts around Swindon, could not deduct the hotel or the Melrose-Swindon travel, because he had chosen Swindon as a base for better pay and shorter journeys. HMRC conceded, and the FTT agreed, that going somewhere for a specific subcontract would have been deductible ([18]). His penalty was cut to 0% as an innocent mistake in a grey area made after taking advice and keeping proper records ([21]).
cases.relevance: The closest recent analogy for a crew member who stays in one city for a season and picks up several jobs there: a hotel for a specific job away from home is fine; a standing base away from home is not, and a hotel chosen for personal convenience is a personal choice ([18]). Taking advice and keeping records protects against penalties even if a claim fails.
cases.status: Good law as an FTT decision (persuasive only). No appeal found on Find Case Law. It applies the Healy UT principles at [66] and Newsom v Robertson ([15]) and distinguishes Horton v Young ([19]).

cases.name: Newsom v Robertson (Inspector of Taxes)
cases.court: Court of Appeal (Somervell, Romer and Denning LJJ)
cases.principle: Travel between home and the place where the profession is carried on is a living expense, not a business expense, even if substantial work is done at home: its object is not to enable a man to do his work but to live away from it (Romer LJ). Denning LJ framed this as identifying the base of operations.
cases.relevance: Doing invoicing, prep or emails at home does not make home the base where the crew member has a fixed or regular place of work elsewhere (a regular venue or a client's workshop); home to there is commuting.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in BIM37605, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Jackman (Inspector of Taxes) v Powell (often cited as Powell v Jackman)
cases.principle: A franchised milkman's daily travel from home to the depot, where he collected his float and stock, was not deductible even though all his office work was done at home: his places of work were predictable, a base can be an area rather than a point, and the statutory test, not identifying a base, is what matters.
cases.relevance: If one client requires the crew member to report regularly to the same yard, warehouse or depot to collect a vehicle or kit before going to sites, that depot is likely the working place and home to depot is commuting. Unpredictable venues fall under Horton; a fixed, recurring place under Jackman.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in BIM37635, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Watkis (Inspector of Taxes) v Ashford, Sparkes and Harward
cases.principle: Partners' food at regular lunchtime and evening meetings was not deductible because they would have eaten anyway, but the accommodation, food and drink at the firm's annual residential conference were, because the overnight stay served the business and any private benefit was incidental.
cases.relevance: Supports deducting a hotel plus meals when a job genuinely requires an overnight stay away from home; meals at routine local meetings (production meetings, crew lunches near home) are not deductible.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in BIM37925, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Sargent (Inspector of Taxes) v Barnes
cases.principle: A dentist who stopped every day at his laboratory between home and surgery could not deduct the journey: interrupting a commute for a business task does not alter the quality of the journey, and 'necessary' is not the statutory test.
cases.relevance: With a regular place of business, calling at a hire company or supplier on the way does not make the commute deductible. If the crew member is itinerant with home as base, the trip is deductible anyway.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in BIM37630, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Prior (Inspector of Taxes) v Saunders
cases.court: High Court (Chancery Division), Sir Mervyn Davies
cases.principle: A self-employed ceiling-fixer who worked mainly in London for years could not deduct his London rent, even the part said to be for storing tools, because it was paid principally as rent for his accommodation; nor could he deduct his food.
cases.relevance: On long engagements in one place, the digs become a living cost. Storing kit in personal accommodation does not make the rent deductible.
cases.status: Good law (not overruled) but fact-specific; HMRC still relies on it in BIM37665.
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in BIM37665, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened. A claim that the Upper Tribunal in Healy discussed it at [58]-[59] could not be confirmed.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Sean Reed v HMRC
cases.court: First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), Judge Jennifer Trigger and Peter Whitehead
cases.principle: An itinerant scaffolder whose home and base were in Grimsby, working at sites across the country, could deduct his travel and the rent of cheap Birmingham accommodation used when working there, because it was a cheaper alternative to hotels and not a base; his home was the only constant feature of his working life ([21]).
cases.relevance: Supports using a short let or digs instead of hotels on away jobs, provided home stays the genuine base and the work really is itinerant. Cited by the UT in Healy at [62] and as an example in principle (2) at [66].
cases.status: Good law (FTT decision, persuasive only). Cited approvingly in HMRC v Healy [2013] UKUT 337 (TCC) at [62] and [66(2)].

cases.name: Timothy David Hanlin v HMRC
cases.court: First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), Judge Kevin Poole and David Kippest
cases.principle: A Coventry-based subcontractor who worked full-time at Dungeness power station for years, staying four nights a week, could not deduct weekly travel, bed and breakfast or evening meals: his base was Dungeness, the travel was partly to keep living at home, and accommodation and meals follow the travel ([32], [42]).
cases.relevance: A long engagement with one client at one place can move the base there, and hotel and meal claims then fall away. Its principles at [28]-[31] include an exception for an emergency call-out from home. The UT in Healy relied on it for principle (7): the longer the stay, the more likely a private purpose.
cases.status: Good law (FTT decision, persuasive only; not overruled). The UT in Healy discussed it at [63]-[65], [66](7) and [77] but warned against reading it as a general rule.

cases.name: Mr Paul Mellor v HMRC
cases.principle: A self-employed electrician who received drawings and prepared quotes at home, kept his tools and records there and worked at varying sites had his base at home, so home-to-site travel was deductible in principle; the burden was still on him to prove the journeys actually made ([17]-[18]).
cases.relevance: Close to a crew member who quotes, negotiates and preps from home and keeps kit there, but it predates Samadian, which narrowed Horton, so give it limited weight and keep a strong mileage log.
cases.status: Good law (FTT, not binding; not overruled), but read subject to Samadian [2014] UKUT 13 (TCC).

cases.name: Noel White v HMRC
cases.court: First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), Judge Greg Sinfield and Mrs Shameem Akhtar
cases.principle: A home-based self-employed flying instructor who almost always worked at the same two airports, with no office there, could not deduct home-to-airport travel: following Samadian, the travel was partly the result of living away from the places where he worked.
cases.relevance: Regular work at the same one or two venues (a resident arena, studio or theatre) defeats home-base travel claims, even with a home office, no office at the venue and bookings taken at home.
cases.status: Good law (FTT decision, persuasive only). Applies Samadian and distinguishes Horton v Young.
cases.note: No reversal found, but a final search for an onward appeal was not completed.

cases.name: Mohammed Maasher v HMRC
cases.court: First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), Judge Jennifer Dean and Susan Stott
cases.principle: A self-employed Arabic interpreter's travel and subsistence between courts, police stations and solicitors' offices were accepted as wholly and exclusively for business; having accepted his Salisbury accommodation was for business, HMRC could not logically refuse the travel to get there ([93]-[97]). HMRC's unexplained recalculations failed against credible, documented evidence. Appeal allowed in part.
cases.relevance: The most recent decision found (June 2026): credible, consistent records (tickets, statements) win, and if a hotel for a job is accepted as business, the travel to that job should follow. Low precedent weight: it cites no case law and turns on its facts.
cases.status: Good law as an FTT decision only (not binding, fact-specific). Find Case Law on 24 Nov 2026 showed no Upper Tribunal decision; the 56-day permission window from release on 18 June 2026 appears to have passed. Quantum and the penalty were left to be agreed or decided at a further hearing ([107]).

cases.name: Hall (HM Inspector of Taxes) v Lorimer
cases.citation: [1993] EWCA Civ 25; [1994] 1 WLR 209 (CA); 66 TC 349; first instance [1992] 1 WLR 939 (Mummery J)
cases.court: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), Nolan LJ
cases.principle: Employment status is decided by painting a picture from the accumulation of detail and then standing back to judge the whole, not by running through a checklist. A freelance vision mixer doing 120-150 engagements a year (the longest 10 days) for about 20 production companies was self-employed, even though he worked in their studios on their equipment.
cases.relevance: The closest authority to this user: a behind-camera technician doing short bookings for many production companies can be self-employed even when the client supplies the kit and venue. HMRC's ESM4120 and ESM4116 adopt it for crew roles and engagements of 10 days or less. Keep evidence of the Lorimer factors: number of clients, short bookings, home office, business-like booking and invoicing, bad-debt risk and own business costs.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL supplied is HMRC v Atholl House Productions [2022] EWCA Civ 501, which discusses and applies Hall v Lorimer; the 1993 judgment itself was not opened. HMRC's summary of the Lorimer factors is at ESM0551 (guidance id esm0551).
cases.source_note: The link is to HMRC v Atholl House Productions [2022] EWCA Civ 501, which applies it; the original judgment was not checked.

cases.name: Ready Mixed Concrete (South East) Ltd v Minister of Pensions and National Insurance
cases.court: High Court (Queen's Bench Division), MacKenna J
cases.principle: A contract of service exists if (i) the worker agrees to provide their own work and skill for pay, (ii) is subject to the other party's control to a sufficient degree, and (iii) the other terms are consistent with employment. An owner-driver who bought and maintained his own lorry and could appoint a substitute was a small businessman, not an employee.
cases.relevance: Tribunals apply this three-stage test to every booking. For a technician, personal work for a day rate usually satisfies stage 1 and a production's framework of control often satisfies stage 2, so status normally turns on stage 3: own substantial kit, financial risk, multiple clients and any real right to send a substitute.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in ESM7030, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Market Investigations Ltd v Minister of Social Security
cases.court: High Court (Queen's Bench Division), Cooke J
cases.principle: The fundamental question is whether the person performs the services as a person in business on their own account, weighing control, own equipment, hiring helpers, financial risk, responsibility for investment and management, and the chance to profit from sound management. A casual market-research interviewer with no obligation to accept work was still employed under each assignment she took.
cases.relevance: Freedom to turn work down does not by itself make each booking self-employed. The business-on-own-account factors are what this user can evidence: own kit and insurance, own rates, bad-debt risk, marketing, and paying own helpers or crew.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in ESM7040, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: Fall (Inspector of Taxes) v Hitchen
cases.principle: A professional performer can be employed under one contract and self-employed under others; a ballet dancer on a standard full-time repertory contract, paid a steady wage whether or not called to perform, held an employment.
cases.relevance: The counterweight to Hall v Lorimer for long single-client engagements: a long, full-time, regularly paid contract with one production company can be employment even if all other work is self-employed. Compare Atholl House CA at [128]: it is the capacity and conditions of the work that matter, not the activities.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL is HMRC's summary in ESM7055, not the judgment; the judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is HMRC’s own summary of the case in its manual; the judgment itself was not checked.

cases.name: HMRC v Professional Game Match Officials Ltd
cases.court: UK Supreme Court (Lord Hodge, Lord Leggatt, Lord Stephens, Lady Rose, Lord Richards; judgment of Lord Richards, 16 September 2024)
cases.principle: Each engagement is tested on its own: mutuality of obligation can exist for the length of a single booking even with no obligation to offer or accept work between bookings, and a right to cancel before the work starts is irrelevant at stage 1 ([40]-[59]). Control can take the form of a framework of contractual obligations about conduct and performance with sanctions applied afterwards; it does not require the ability to step in during the work ([76], [88]).
cases.relevance: Separate POs per job with no obligation between them do not stop each booking being an employment, and nor does a production's inability to direct a skilled technician. Never reason 'no mutuality, therefore self-employed'; for this user the decisive ground is stage 3 (in business on own account, own equipment, financial risk, multiple clients).
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Professional Game Match Officials Ltd v HMRC (remitted hearing)
cases.court: First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), Judge Geraint Williams and Dr Phebe Mann; judgment 1 May 2026
cases.principle: Even with the irreducible minimum of mutuality and control held present by the Supreme Court, the stage 3 multi-factor evaluation pointed to self-employment: obligations were narrow, episodic and voluntary (referees could decline or withdraw), control was regulatory, developmental and gatekeeping rather than managerial, the referees had substantial autonomy, and there was no economic dependency (no salary, retainer or guaranteed income). 'This is not a finely balanced case' ([314]); the match engagements were contracts for services ([317]).
cases.relevance: The most recent application of the Supreme Court's test. Pay per booking, no retainer, freedom to decline, autonomy in the technical work, several clients, and own kit and risk support self-employment; the app can help keep evidence of these. The referees had full-time jobs elsewhere, whereas this user depends far more on production work.
cases.status: Good law as an FTT decision (persuasive only, fact-specific).
cases.note: Para 320 gives the 56-day window to apply for permission to appeal; whether HMRC applied is not confirmed from an official source.

cases.name: HMRC v Atholl House Productions Ltd
cases.court: Court of Appeal (Civil Division): Peter Jackson LJ, Arnold LJ, Sir David Richards; 26 April 2022
cases.principle: Ready Mixed Concrete and Hall v Lorimer are not separate tests: once mutuality and control are present, the tribunal weighs all relevant factors, limited to the contract terms and circumstances known or reasonably known to both parties ([122]-[123]). A worker's known business on own account must not be ignored, but other engagements are not a gold standard, and the same person can be employed under one contract and self-employed under another ([124], [128]-[129]). The Autoclenz approach does not apply to tax status ([152]-[157]).
cases.relevance: The user's wider freelance business helps but does not decide the status of a particular long engagement. Review that engagement's own terms (length, exclusivity, first call on time, substitution, paid holiday, fixed fee) and what the production company knew.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Atholl House Productions Ltd v HMRC (remitted hearing)
cases.court: First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), Judge Tony Beare; released 29 November 2023
cases.principle: Applying the Court of Appeal's guidance, the FTT again held that Kaye Adams's hypothetical contracts with BBC Radio Scotland would have been contracts for services, not employment, and allowed the appeal ([174]).
cases.relevance: The Court of Appeal's approach can still give a self-employed result for a long-running media engagement where the worker has a genuine freelance practice and the terms support it (described as a freelance contributor, non-exclusive in practice, paid per programme).
cases.status: Good law (FTT decision, not binding; no onward appeal found on Find Case Law).

cases.name: Kickabout Productions Ltd v HMRC
cases.court: Court of Appeal (Civil Division): Peter Jackson LJ, Arnold LJ, Sir David Richards; 26 April 2022
cases.principle: What counts is the contractual right of control, not how much it is used: talkSPORT's ultimate right to decide a show's form and content was enough control despite the presenter's wide practical freedom ([84]); his renewable contracts to co-present every weekday were employment under IR35 ([106]).
cases.relevance: A technician's skill and day-to-day freedom do not rule out control; the production company's right to decide what is done, where and when still counts. Long, renewable engagements with one client expected to provide regular work weigh towards employment.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Christa Ackroyd Media Ltd v HMRC
cases.court: Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber), Mann J and Judge Thomas Scott; 25 October 2019
cases.principle: Control concerns whether ultimate authority over the worker lay with the engager, not whether day-to-day control was exercised; having no line manager or appraisals does not prevent a sufficient framework of control. Control imposed for regulatory reasons (BBC Editorial Guidelines and programme-standards obligations) still counts, so IR35 applied to a 7-year fixed-term contract giving the BBC first call on up to 225 days a year.
cases.relevance: Industry rules an engager can enforce on the user (health and safety, broadcaster technical standards, venue rules) can count towards control; but a long, near-exclusive seven-year contract is very different from short PO-based jobs.
cases.status: Good law (Upper Tribunal; not a Court of Appeal decision).

cases.name: Paya Ltd and others v HMRC (BBC presenters Joanna Gosling, David Eades and Tim Willcox)
cases.principle: IR35 applied to the presenters' service companies (except some of Tim Willcox Ltd's BBC World contracts), on the judge's casting vote with one member dissenting. HMRC had not proved the advisers careless, and an accountant was not careless merely because a difficult judgement later proved wrong, so the extended time limit in TMA s36(1B) did not apply and PAYE regulation 80 determinations for earlier years were out of time. Appeals allowed in part.
cases.relevance: Limited for a crew member: presenters on regular rolling contracts with one broadcaster are usually caught. Taking proper advice can protect against penalties and extended time limits even when the status argument is lost.
cases.status: Good law as an FTT decision (binds no one). No appeal found; later FTT decisions cite it (Alan Parry Productions [2022] UKFTT 194 (TC) at [616]). On status the appellate authorities now govern (Atholl House [2022] EWCA Civ 501; PGMOL [2024] UKSC 29).

cases.name: Red White and Green Ltd v HMRC (Eamonn Holmes)
cases.court: Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber), Mellor J and Judge Jonathan Cannan; 29 March 2023
cases.principle: Control covers what, how, where and when, and editorial and regulatory control (such as Ofcom compliance) are relevant even though they apply to employed and self-employed alike ([43]-[55]). For 'in business on own account', the tribunal looks at the particular engagement and may weigh heavy dependence on one client and the absence of business features (fixed fee, no financial risk, client-provided expenses and equipment) ([110]-[116], [137(2)]). IR35 applied to Mr Holmes's This Morning work for 2011-12 to 2014-15.
cases.relevance: Even an autonomous presenter with other commercial activities was an employee under regular fixed-fee contracts with one broadcaster; a regular block of work for one client on fixed terms can be employment whatever happens elsewhere in the user's business.
cases.status: Good law. No onward appeal reported; consistent with Atholl House, Kickabout and PGMOL [2024] UKSC 29.
cases.note: A search for a Court of Appeal decision was not completed.

cases.name: HMRC v Basic Broadcasting Ltd (Adrian Chiles)
cases.court: Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber); 7 June 2024
cases.principle: 'In business on own account' can be used to test the contract in question or to describe the person's work outside it; a business outside the contract is an important contextual circumstance but no more than that, and its weight is for the FTT ([48]). HMRC's appeal was allowed and the case remitted on stage 3.
cases.relevance: This user's established multi-client trade is relevant context for any single long engagement, but not decisive; the terms of that engagement must still be weighed.
cases.status: Good law. Remitted to the FTT; no remitted decision found on Find Case Law.

cases.name: HMRC v S & L Barnes Ltd (Stuart Barnes)
cases.court: Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber); 28 August 2024
cases.principle: The UT remade the decision: a long fixed term (four years, extendable by two), no right of substitution, Sky's first call on up to 228 days a year, exclusivity as a UK broadcaster and no financial risk together outweighed Mr Barnes's freelance business outside Sky, so his Sky engagement was employment.
cases.relevance: Lists the terms that tip a long engagement into employment. If a production company offers a long contract, check for a fixed term of months or years, first call on the user's time, exclusivity, required personal service and a guaranteed fee.
cases.status: Good law. No onward appeal on Find Case Law; cited in PD & MJ [2025] UKUT 94 (TCC) and George Mantides [2025] UKUT 124 (TCC).

cases.name: PD & MJ Ltd v HMRC (Phil Thompson, Sky Soccer Saturday)
cases.court: Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber); 17 March 2025
cases.principle: IR35 appeal dismissed: a regular pundit would have been Sky's employee under hypothetical direct contracts. Relying on the exact 80% share of his income, which Sky could not have known, was an immaterial error, because financial dependence during the contract and Sky's knowledge that this was his only broadcasting contract were relevant ([195]-[196]). The chance to earn more by using his time well was neutral on the facts ([198]-[200]).
cases.relevance: Being able to take other work does not by itself make a regular engagement self-employed; what counts is risk and reward within that engagement.
cases.status: Good law as far as verified.
cases.note: A search for any appeal to the Court of Appeal was not completed.

cases.name: Uber BV v Aslam
cases.principle: For statutory 'worker' (limb (b)) rights the written agreement is not the starting point: the legislation is interpreted purposively and applied to the facts viewed realistically, focusing on control and subordination. Uber drivers were workers.
cases.relevance: Employment-law contrast only: 'worker' status (holiday pay, minimum wage) has no tax equivalent. Tax and NIC use a two-way common-law test, employee or self-employed (PGMOL [2024] UKSC 29 at [2]-[3]). A technician could be a worker for employment rights yet self-employed for tax; do not mix the two.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Autoclenz Ltd v Belcher
cases.principle: In employment-rights claims (National Minimum Wage, Working Time Regulations), a tribunal may set aside written terms that do not reflect what the parties really agreed; given unequal bargaining power the true agreement is found from all the circumstances, of which the written contract is only part ([35]).
cases.relevance: A PO or crew booking terms saying 'freelance', or an unused substitution clause, will not decide status if reality differs, and the user cannot rely on labels either. Ask how each job works in practice (HMRC ESM0510).
cases.status: Good law but limited in scope: Uber [2021] UKSC 5 at [69]-[78] explains it as purposive statutory interpretation, and the Court of Appeal in Atholl House [2022] EWCA Civ 501 at [152]-[157] held it does not apply to IR35 / ITEPA s49 tax-status questions, where ordinary contract interpretation applies.

cases.name: HMRC v Tooth
cases.principle: A 'deliberate inaccuracy' (TMA s118(7), which opens the 20-year limit) means a statement the taxpayer knew was wrong and intended to mislead HMRC with (recklessness left open, [47]); a deliberate choice that turns out wrong is not enough, and each entry is read against the whole return. A discovery is the officer's own new realisation, needs no new facts, does not go stale through HMRC delay ([75]-[76]), and is not defeated because other officers already knew.
cases.relevance: An honest, explained position on the return (hotel costs on a long engagement, the business share of car costs) cannot be reached back 20 years as 'deliberate'. HMRC delay after a discovery does not void an assessment made in time: disclosure helps; waiting for HMRC to go quiet does not.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Christine Perrin v HMRC
cases.principle: HMRC must first prove with evidence that a penalty is prima facie due ([69]); only then must the taxpayer prove a reasonable excuse on the balance of probabilities ([70]). The test is objective but takes account of the taxpayer's experience, attributes and situation, in four stages ([81]): facts asserted, facts proven, whether they objectively amount to a reasonable excuse and when it ended, and whether the failure was remedied without unreasonable delay. Ignorance of a requirement can be an excuse if objectively reasonable for that taxpayer ([82]).
cases.relevance: The working framework for appealing late-filing or late-payment penalties (touring, venue Wi-Fi failures, illness, a missed HMRC letter). Collect dated evidence for each stage and act fast once the excuse ends. HMRC adopts it in CH160950.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Donaldson v HMRC
cases.principle: HMRC can decide by general policy, in advance, that everyone more than 3 months late gets £10-a-day penalties (Sch 55 para 4), and standard SA reminders can give the required notice, even before the default ([21]). The penalty notice should state the period ([26]), but omitting it was a defect of form saved by TMA s114, so the penalties stood ([29]).
cases.relevance: A return more than 3 months late costs £100 plus up to £900 in daily penalties. Technical attacks on HMRC's automated process rarely work, so push on-time filing (31 January) rather than procedural defences.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Burgess and Brimheath Developments Ltd v HMRC
cases.principle: In a discovery assessment appeal HMRC bear the burden of proving the assessment was validly made: that there was a discovery, that the s29(4)/(5) conditions are met, and that any extended time limit (careless or deliberate conduct) applies; the taxpayer bears the burden only on the amount. The assessments were reduced to nil without remittal.
cases.relevance: If HMRC raise a late (out-of-enquiry) assessment, first check whether they can prove the discovery, the carelessness or deliberate conduct, and the 4/6/20-year limit; a legitimate defence that can remove the tax entirely.
cases.status: Good law. Followed in HMRC v Jafari [2022] UKUT 119 (TCC) at [16]-[17] and Danapal v HMRC [2023] UKUT 86 (TCC) at [12]; explained and distinguished in Kingston Maurward College [2023] UKUT 69 (TCC) at [32]. HMRC v Harte [2026] UKUT 112 (TCC) states the same two-stage burden at [46] but does not cite it.

cases.name: HMRC v Harte
cases.court: Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber); 11 March 2026
cases.principle: Where one discovery assessment for a year covers several separate errors, each loss of tax must separately meet the conduct condition (s29(4)) and its own 4, 6 or 20-year limit (ss34, 36). Proving one deliberate error does not let HMRC sweep careless or innocent errors in under the 20-year limit, and amounts that fail are removed as overcharges (TMA s50(6)).
cases.relevance: Facts close to this user's: a self-employed consultant with undeclared receipts, vehicle capital allowances, a home-office claim and card spending. An honest mistake made despite reasonable care cannot be assessed outside the enquiry window, and careless errors are capped at 6 years even when another error was deliberate.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Clark v HMRC
cases.principle: A discovery assessment's scope is set by the loss of tax the officer actually discovered, read in context (including enquiry correspondence), and cannot be widened during the appeal ([106]), although HMRC may put new arguments for the same conclusion.
cases.relevance: If HMRC assess, check what the officer actually identified: an assessment about mileage claims cannot later be stretched to cover unrelated income. The officer's letters define the battleground.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Langham (Inspector of Taxes) v Veltema
cases.principle: Under TMA s29(5), HMRC are barred from a discovery assessment only if the information made available under s29(6) (the return and accompanying documents, claims, enquiry documents, written notifications and reasonable inferences) would have made a hypothetical officer aware of an actual insufficiency; information that would only prompt checks is not enough (Auld LJ, [33]-[36]).
cases.relevance: A legal way to shorten exposure: explain contestable positions in the return's white space (for example treating a long single-client engagement as temporary workplaces, or the car-cost method) so HMRC must enquire within the s9A window or lose the point, unless the return was careless or deliberate.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Atherton v HMRC
cases.principle: For s29(4) the question is whether the taxpayer and those acting on his behalf took reasonable care to avoid the insufficiency (TMA s118(5)); an agent's carelessness counts against the taxpayer ([61]-[63]), though reasonable reliance on advice from someone not acting on the taxpayer's behalf may avoid carelessness ([63]).
cases.relevance: A careless return filed by an accountant opens a 6-year assessment window (s36(1B)), even though the freelancer may escape an inaccuracy penalty by showing personal reasonable care (FA 2007 Sch 24 para 18(3)). Review figures before filing.
cases.status: Good law on carelessness. Its assumption (at [17]-[19]) that a staleness doctrine could apply is superseded by HMRC v Tooth [2021] UKSC 17 at [75]-[77], which held there is none.

cases.name: Barry Edwards v HMRC
cases.principle: Penalty appeals are treated as criminal for Article 6 purposes, so HMRC must prove the facts a penalty depends on, including that a s8 notice to file was sent ([38]). Sch 55 penalties are not disproportionate just because no tax turns out to be due, so that cannot be a 'special circumstance' ([84]-[87]); the tribunal can interfere with HMRC's special-circumstances decision only if it was flawed.
cases.relevance: Once HMRC issue a notice to file, the freelancer must file even in a nil or loss year, or ask HMRC to withdraw the notice (TMA s8B) rather than ignore it. Disputing receipt of the notice puts HMRC to proof.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Harrison v HMRC
cases.principle: A reasonable excuse must exist at the filing date ([31]) and the return must then be filed without unreasonable delay once it ends (Sch 55 para 23(2)(c)). Mental ill-health can be an excuse but depends on evidence ([36]-[39]); an excuse based on a former accountant's failure ended when the taxpayer learned of it. A 12-month 'deliberate but not concealed' penalty of £42,066.09 was upheld, and 'special circumstances' needs no gloss beyond 'special' ([57]).
cases.relevance: A busy touring schedule will not excuse a late return if the freelancer kept working. Medical or bereavement excuses need contemporaneous evidence. Very late returns can attract tax-geared penalties far above the fixed £100/£300 amounts.
cases.status: Good law (not overruled or doubted as far as checked). Sch 55 governs SA late filing for 2023-24 to 2025-26; MTD-mandated taxpayers move to the FA 2021 Sch 24 points regime from 2026-27, with a similar reasonable-excuse test.

cases.name: HMRC v Hok Ltd
cases.principle: The FTT's powers are wholly statutory: it can cancel a penalty that was not incurred or correct its amount, but cannot cancel or reduce a penalty because HMRC acted unfairly, for example by sending late reminders ([36]), and it has no judicial review jurisdiction ([41]).
cases.relevance: Penalty appeals must rest on statutory grounds (no liability, reasonable excuse, a flawed special-circumstances decision, wrong amount); 'HMRC were unfair' alone fails.
cases.status: Good law on the principle; the specific TMA s98A/P35 penalty regime in the case has since been replaced.

cases.name: Martland v HMRC
cases.principle: Permission to appeal late starts from the position that it should not be granted unless the FTT is satisfied it should. The FTT considers the length of the delay, the reasons, and all the circumstances balancing prejudice to both sides ([44]), giving particular weight to efficient litigation and respecting time limits ([45]), without a mini-trial of the merits ([46]).
cases.relevance: The appeal window is normally 30 days (TMA s31A); late appeals need HMRC's agreement (s49) or tribunal permission and are hard to win. Flag appeal deadlines the moment a decision letter arrives.
cases.status: Good law. Medpro [2025] UKUT 255 (TCC), on a casting vote, held the extra-weight guidance impermissible under VATA s83G(6); the Court of Appeal reversed that in HMRC v MedPro [2026] EWCA Civ 14 and endorsed Martland as amplified by Katib (non-binding guidance the FTT may depart from for sound reasons).

cases.name: HMRC v Katib
cases.principle: On late appeals, an adviser's failures are generally treated as the taxpayer's own because statutory time limits matter ([54]); adviser incompetence, however spectacular, does not help ([58]), and the remedy is a damages claim against the adviser ([59]). Being misled by an adviser is not an exception in itself but is relevant at the Martland balancing stage ([56]).
cases.relevance: Even with an accountant, the freelancer remains responsible for deadlines; the app should track filing and appeal deadlines itself and prompt the user.
cases.status: Good law. Approved generally by the Court of Appeal in HMRC v MedPro [2026] EWCA Civ 14 at [57], [59]; applied in Cenkci v HMRC [2026] UKUT 249 (TCC) at [27]-[30].
cases.note: A claimed application in 'Uddin [2023] UKUT 99 (TCC)' could not be verified (Find Case Law 404); do not cite it.

cases.name: HMRC v MedPro Healthcare Ltd & Ors
cases.court: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), Lewison LJ (Whipple and Miles LJJ agreeing); 19 January 2026
cases.principle: A superior court or tribunal may give guidance on how the FTT should exercise its discretion to allow a late appeal (here VATA s83G(6)), including giving particular weight to some factors; the guidance is not binding and the FTT may depart from it for sound reasons ([45]). The Martland three-stage test as amplified in Katib is appropriate ([57], [59]), and 'a time limit is not simply a target date; it is there to be respected' ([43]).
cases.relevance: The latest authority on late tax appeals: missing the 30-day window is serious and blaming an adviser rarely helps. Treat appeal deadlines as hard.
cases.status: Good law as checked, subject to any Supreme Court appeal. Reverses [2025] UKUT 255 (TCC) on ground 4 only.

cases.name: HMRC v Raftopoulou
cases.principle: The reasonable-excuse deeming in TMA s118(2) covers mandatory acts, not conditions attached to voluntary rights such as claims; it relieves the consequences of failing to act but does not treat the act as done ([64]-[66]), so it cannot extend the 4-year overpayment relief limit (Sch 1AB) and has no general time-extending role ([68]).
cases.relevance: Missed expenses must be claimed in time: amend within 12 months of the filing date (s9ZA) or claim overpayment relief within 4 years of the end of the tax year (Sch 1AB, subject to its exclusions, e.g. missed capital allowance claims). 2022-23 claims close on 5 April 2027 and reasonable excuse will not reopen them.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Carmel Jordan v HMRC
cases.principle: A taxpayer cannot appeal a requirement in a Sch 36 taxpayer notice to produce statutory records (the business records they must keep under TMA s12B) (FA 2008 Sch 36 para 29(2)), and the FTT's decision on a Sch 36 appeal is final (para 32(5)).
cases.relevance: In a records check or enquiry, invoices, receipts, mileage logs, bank records and PO paperwork must be produced on request; disputes are limited to non-statutory items. Complete, exportable records are the best protection.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: HMRC v Rogers and Shaw
cases.principle: A s8 notice to file need not be issued by an identified, flesh-and-blood HMRC officer, so automated notices are valid; but in a penalty appeal the tribunal can consider whether a valid notice to file was given.
cases.relevance: Arguments that a computer-generated notice is invalid fail; but if a notice to file was genuinely never received, there is no failure under s8 and HMRC must prove it was given.
cases.status: Good law. The officer point is also fixed by Finance Act 2020 s103 (HMRC functions may be exercised by computer, naming s8 notices; treated as always in force, with a narrow exception for unappealed rulings before 11 March 2020). The jurisdiction holding follows HMRC v Goldsmith [2019] UKUT 325 (TCC).
cases.note: A full later-case check was not completed.

cases.name: Hayes v HMRC
cases.principle: HMRC's Covid-era waiver of late-filing penalties for 2019-20 returns filed by 28 February 2021 did not extend the 31 January deadline, so a February return was late and HMRC's enquiry window was extended under TMA s9A(2)(b). Following Raftopoulou, s118(2) gives no general power to extend time, and public-law fairness complaints belong in judicial review.
cases.relevance: Filing by 31 January keeps HMRC's enquiry window at 12 months from filing; filing late, even inside a penalty easement, extends it to the quarter day after the first anniversary of filing.
cases.status: Good law (UT decision refusing permission to appeal after an oral hearing; persuasive, not binding precedent).

cases.name: HMRC v Wilkes
cases.principle: Under the old wording of TMA s29(1)(a) ('income which ought to have been assessed'), HMRC could not raise discovery assessments for the High Income Child Benefit Charge, because the charge is not income ([29], [36]-[38]).
cases.relevance: Now largely closed: FA 2022 s97 rewrote s29(1)(a) to cover 'an amount of income tax or capital gains tax', retrospectively, so discovery reaches HICBC if the user or a partner claims Child Benefit and income passes the threshold.
cases.status: Superseded by statute: FA 2022 s97 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2022/3/section/97), except for protected assessments whose appeal was notified by 30 June 2021 on the not-income ground, or was stayed before 27 October 2021 partly for that reason.

cases.name: Seven Individuals v HMRC
cases.court: Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber), Nugee J
cases.principle: 'Commercial basis' (ITA 2007 ss66(2)(a), 74(2)(a)) has an objective element: a trade is commercial only if run the way people seriously interested in profit would run it; good organisation plus a subjective hope of profit is not enough, and the likelihood of profit is central ([46]-[47], [54]). Icebreaker LLP loss schemes failed.
cases.relevance: A loss-making trade or sideline claiming s64 or s72 relief must be run on commercial lines (realistic pricing, marketing, records, a real prospect of profit). Loss-generating investment schemes fail; never suggest them.
cases.status: Good law on the commerciality limb (cited in Naghshineh [2022] EWCA Civ 19 at [16] and Macdonald [2025] UKFTT 495 (TC)). On the separate view-to-profit limb it has been refined: Ingenious Games ([2019] UKUT 226 (TCC); [2021] EWCA Civ 1180 at [122]) treats that limb as wholly subjective.
cases.note: A full citator check was not completed.

cases.name: Beacon v HMRC
cases.principle: A sole trader's Tuscan villa hospitality business that made heavy early losses after being blown off course by the 2008 recession was still carried on commercially and with a view to profit under ITA s66, so s64 relief was allowed for 2010-11 and 2011-12. HMRC's contentions (no business plan, poor records, non-commercial pricing, hobby use) failed for want of evidence; a bank-approved business plan existed ([43]-[48]).
cases.relevance: Supports a s64 claim where losses come from a market downturn (for example an events-sector slump) rather than an uncommercial set-up. Keep evidence: pricing, bookings, marketing and a plan.
cases.status: FTT decision, persuasive only and fact-specific. No appeal or overruling found; cited in Macdonald [2025] UKFTT 495 (TC). s66(2) now reads 'throughout the tax year' from 2024-25 (FA 2022 Sch 1), which does not affect the principle.

cases.name: Charlotte Macdonald v HMRC
cases.court: First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), Judge Natsai Manyarara and Duncan McBride
cases.principle: The two limbs of s66(2) are cumulative: a shoot run on a commercial basis still failed because it was not carried on with a view to profit. Losses over several years do not by themselves make a trade uncommercial ([94]), but a reality check applies: an activity that hardly made a profit in over 15 years lacked a view to profit ([105]-[115]).
cases.relevance: Repeated sideways claims for a long-running loss-making sideline become very hard to sustain; after several loss years, suggest carry-forward or restructuring the activity instead.
cases.status: Good law as an FTT decision (does not bind other tribunals). Follows Ingenious Games in treating the view-to-profit limb as subjective ([105]).
cases.note: Find Case Law showed no Upper Tribunal appeal, but appeal status could not be fully confirmed.

cases.name: Wannell v Rothwell (HMIT)
cases.court: High Court (Chancery Division), Robert Walker J
cases.principle: 'Commercial' is the opposite of 'uncommercial': a trade is uncommercial if its terms (prices that ignore costs) or its conduct (hours at the owner's whim) are. The line falls between the serious trader seriously interested in profit, whatever their shortcomings, and the amateur or dilettante.
cases.relevance: The classic test HMRC (BIM85705) and tribunals still apply when deciding whether a loss-making activity gets sideways relief.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL is Seven Individuals v HMRC [2017] UKUT 132 (TCC), which quotes and applies Wannell; the 1996 judgment itself was not opened. HMRC also applies it in BIM85705.
cases.source_note: The link is to Seven Individuals v HMRC [2017] UKUT 132 (TCC), which applies it; the original judgment was not checked.

cases.name: Ardeshir Naghshineh v HMRC
cases.court: Court of Appeal (Whipple LJ, Green LJ, Birss LJ)
cases.principle: Loss-relief restrictions are cumulative. The farming 'reasonable expectation of profit' test in ITA s68(3)(b) is wholly objective, judged from a competent farmer's viewpoint, unlike s66, which has objective and subjective elements ([16], [21], [45], [50], [81]).
cases.relevance: Mostly background: passing one loss test does not pass the others. The farming rule itself does not apply to this freelancer.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: JJK Engineering Ltd v HMRC
cases.principle: On a Flat Rate Scheme decision the tribunal asks whether HMRC could reasonably have been satisfied there were grounds for it (VATA s84(4ZA)); HMRC's policy of not backdating a sector change from a reasonable original choice is itself reasonable, and the test is whether the choice was reasonable, not correct ([43]-[51]). A mechanical engineer put in the higher 'architect, civil or structural engineer' sector had not made a reasonable choice, so HMRC's refusal to backdate a move to 'any other activity' was quashed ([52]-[57], [81]). Obiter: a VATA s80 overpayment claim (4-year limit) may be available anyway ([69]-[80]).
cases.relevance: If the technician joins the FRS, choose and record a sector that reasonably fits (e.g. 'Any other activity not listed elsewhere' or 'Film, radio, television or video production'); a clearly wrong higher-rate choice can be corrected and backdated.
cases.status: Good law but not binding (FTT, persuasive only); no appeal or disapproval found. Consistent with Idess Ltd [2014] UKFTT 511 (TC) and AML Consulting [2012] UKFTT 474 (TC). VAT Notice 733 para 4.2 restates the HMRC policy the case reviewed; it does not derive from the case.

cases.name: HMRC v Burke
cases.principle: HMRC has a wide discretion over retrospective entry to the flat rate scheme and normally refuses it for periods already accounted for on the normal basis; the tribunal's role over that discretion is supervisory, and HMRC has no duty to tell a trader about the scheme ([19], [21], [44]-[50]).
cases.relevance: Decide on the FRS at registration or before a period's VAT is calculated; do not suggest switching retrospectively after seeing which method gives a lower bill.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Inland Revenue Commissioners v Duke of Westminster
cases.principle: Lord Tomlin: 'Every man is entitled if he can to order his affairs so that the tax attaching under the appropriate Acts is less than it otherwise would be.' A genuine transaction is taxed according to its legal rights and obligations, not some supposed substance, unless the documents are a sham.
cases.relevance: The starting point for legal tax planning: the user may arrange genuine affairs (when to buy kit, which statutory method to use) to pay less tax. It does not protect artificial schemes; modern courts read it narrowly (Ramsay, McGuckian, BMBF) and the GAAR overlays it, so never quote it alone to justify a scheme.
cases.status: Good law (never overruled) but narrowed by the Ramsay principle of purposive construction for avoidance schemes, and by statute (FA 2013 Part 5 GAAR and targeted anti-avoidance rules). Per McGuckian it is no longer canonical as to the consequence of an avoidance scheme.

cases.name: W T Ramsay Ltd v Inland Revenue Commissioners (with Eilbeck v Rawling)
cases.principle: Where a pre-planned, self-cancelling scheme is intended to operate as a whole, the court need not look at each step in blinkers and may tax the composite transaction; artificial capital losses bought off the shelf from a promoter were fiscally ineffective. Lord Wilberforce confirmed a taxpayer may arrange affairs to reduce tax but said the Westminster principle must not be overstated or overextended.
cases.relevance: The origin of the courts' power to look through marketed schemes. Warning signs to spot in anything offered to the user: a ready-made plan bought for a fee, steps run to a timetable, circular money, and no real change in position except the fee.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL supplied is Schofield v HMRC [2012] EWCA Civ 927 (Court of Appeal, 11 July 2012), which discusses and applies Ramsay (checked 24 Nov 2026); the House of Lords judgment itself was not opened at that URL.
cases.source_note: The link is to Schofield v HMRC [2012] EWCA Civ 927, which applies it; the original judgment was not checked.

cases.name: Furniss (Inspector of Taxes) v Dawson
cases.principle: Lord Brightman: where there is a pre-ordained series of transactions and steps are inserted that have no commercial purpose apart from avoiding tax, the inserted steps are disregarded for tax purposes and the end result is taxed. The scheme need not be self-cancelling, and an informal, non-binding arrangement is enough.
cases.relevance: Extended Ramsay to an otherwise genuine commercial deal (an Isle of Man company inserted to defer tax failed). Routing income or purchases through an extra entity, an offshore party or a third-party 'lender' purely for tax will be looked through, even if the underlying work is real.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Inland Revenue Commissioners v McGuckian
cases.court: House of Lords (on appeal from Northern Ireland)
cases.principle: Lord Steyn: the Westminster dictum still points to the citizen's general liberty to arrange financial affairs, but it has ceased to be canonical as to the consequence of a tax avoidance scheme; Ramsay is orthodox purposive interpretation. Lord Browne-Wilkinson: artificial steps inserted only for a tax advantage are disregarded.
cases.relevance: The clearest House of Lords statement of the modern limit on Duke of Westminster: 'it's legal because the documents are genuine' is no defence when a step exists only to get a tax result.
cases.status: Good law, not overruled; the Supreme Court still applies it (UBS [2016] UKSC 13; Rossendale [2021] UKSC 16) as restated in BMBF [2004] UKHL 51.
cases.note: A pin-cite to BMBF para 28 is unverified.

cases.name: Inland Revenue Commissioners v Willoughby
cases.citation: [1997] STC 995 (also commonly cited as [1997] 1 WLR 1071; 70 TC 57)
cases.principle: For the transfer-of-assets motive defence (ICTA 1988 s741), tax avoidance means reducing tax without incurring the economic consequences Parliament intended, whereas tax mitigation means taking a fiscally attractive option the legislation offers and genuinely suffering its consequences, so accepting a freedom from tax Parliament deliberately offered is not avoidance (Revenue counsel's propositions adopted by Lord Nolan).
cases.relevance: The working test for what the assistant helps with: capital allowances on kit really bought, real pension contributions, or choosing a statutory method (simplified mileage, cash basis) is mitigation; a loan scheme, or an 'expense' that does not really cost the user money, is avoidance.
cases.status: Good law but limited in scope: Lord Hoffmann in MacNiven v Westmoreland [2001] UKHL 6 at [62] confined the distinction to statutes that themselves use words like 'avoidance'; it is not a general test of whether a tax-saving step works. The transfer-of-assets rules are now in ITA 2007.
cases.note: The report citations [1997] 1 WLR 1071 and 70 TC 57 were not checked.

cases.name: Barclays Mercantile Business Finance Ltd v Mawson (Inspector of Taxes)
cases.court: House of Lords (Appellate Committee, joint opinion)
cases.principle: Ramsay is not a special tax doctrine: the statute is given a purposive construction and the facts are viewed realistically to see whether they answer the statutory description ([32]); quoting Ribeiro PJ in Arrowtown, the ultimate question is whether the provisions, construed purposively, were intended to apply to the transaction, viewed realistically ([36]). Capital allowances were allowed because the lessor really incurred expenditure on plant for its trade.
cases.relevance: The modern test, applied directly to capital allowances: allowances follow real expenditure on plant or machinery used in the trade. The purposive approach can favour the taxpayer when a transaction genuinely meets the statute, so not every tax-motivated choice is abusive.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The [2005] 1 AC 684 report citation was not checked.

cases.name: HMRC v Tower MCashback LLP 1 and another
cases.principle: LLP members claimed 100% first-year allowances on software rights, paying 25% of the price in cash and 75% through circular, interest-free non-recourse loans that never reached the vendor ([77]). Allowances were due on only 25% ([79]), because the statute requires real expenditure for the real purpose of acquiring plant for a trade ([80]); the court tests the facts, realistically viewed, against the statutory text, purposively construed ([67]).
cases.relevance: A direct warning for equipment claims: allowances (or cash-basis deductions) are on the price actually paid for kit used in the business. Inflated prices, circular finance or 'investment' schemes promising allowances greater than the cash put in will fail.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The [2011] 2 AC 457 report citation was not checked.

cases.name: RFC 2012 plc (in liquidation) (formerly The Rangers Football Club plc) v Advocate General for Scotland
cases.principle: Money paid as a reward for an employee's work is taxable earnings even if, by agreement or acquiescence, it is paid to a third party such as a trust that then 'lends' it to the worker, and PAYE should have been operated ([41], [58]-[59], [67]). The 'loans' did not stop the payments being remuneration.
cases.relevance: The leading authority against disguised remuneration: being paid through a trust, loan or other third party does not make earnings tax-free. Refuse any suggestion to take freelance or contract income as loans, advances or trust payments; for a sole trader the parallel statutory rule is ITTOIA 2005 ss23A-23H.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Hurstwood Properties (A) Ltd and others v Rossendale Borough Council and another
cases.court: UK Supreme Court (Lords Briggs and Leggatt; Lords Reed, Hodge and Kitchin agreeing)
cases.principle: The Ramsay principle has reached well-settled maturity and is not in its essentials particular to tax, resting on the purposive approach to all legislation: whether the provisions, construed purposively, were intended to apply to the transaction viewed realistically ([9], [13]-[15]). Legal certainty does not extend to construing legislation so as to guarantee the effectiveness of transactions undertaken solely to avoid the liability it seeks to impose ([61]). Shell-company tenants in business-rate schemes were arguably not the 'owner', so the claims were reinstated for trial.
cases.relevance: The most recent Supreme Court restatement: as at 2026 courts test artificial arrangements against what Parliament intended, so a clever structure whose only purpose is avoiding a charge is expected to fail.
cases.status: Good law (unanimous). A leading authority alongside BMBF [2004] UKHL 51 and UBS [2016] UKSC 13; its facts concern non-domestic rates, not income tax.
cases.note: The [2022] AC 690 report citation was not checked.

cases.name: Stephen Hoey and others v HMRC
cases.principle: An IT contractor paid largely through EBT 'loans' via offshore employers in a DOTAS-disclosed scheme conceded these were earnings after Rangers. Liability to income tax on employment income rests throughout on the individual ([67]), and where tax is not deducted at source the worker must pay ([82]); HMRC could relieve UK end-users of PAYE duties (ITEPA s684(7A)(b)) and pursue the contractor, a challenge to which lies by judicial review.
cases.relevance: A worker cannot shelter behind a non-compliant umbrella or offshore employer: the tax bill lands on the worker. If the user mentions past or present schemes, say so plainly and point to HMRC's exit and settlement routes.
cases.status: Good law as checked: appeal and cross-appeal dismissed ([205](vi)); judicial review failed ([205](ii)).
cases.note: A further appeal to the Supreme Court was not checked.

cases.name: R v Dimsey
cases.principle: Offshore companies centrally managed and controlled in the UK are UK-resident and liable to corporation tax, and that liability is not removed by the transfer-of-assets rules (ICTA 1988 s739); dishonestly concealing it could support a conspiracy to cheat the public revenue. In the companion case R v Allen [2001] UKHL 45, dishonestly failing to declare income can be cheating the public revenue.
cases.relevance: Concealing income from HMRC is the common-law crime of cheating the public revenue, and advisers and helpers are prosecuted too; supports refusing to help hide income or mislead HMRC, or to help third parties do so.
cases.status: Believed good law (not known to be overruled). The transfer-of-assets rules are now ITA 2007 ss714-751.
cases.note: The researcher stated this summary was from memory and was not checked against the judgment at the URL. Treat as unverified; for the evasion boundary rely primarily on Theft Act 1968 s32, TMA 1970 s106A, R v Mavji and Dosanjh.

cases.name: R v Mavji
cases.principle: Cheating the public revenue does not require a positive act of deceit: it can include any fraudulent conduct that diverts money from the revenue and deprives it of money to which it is entitled, so dishonestly failing to make VAT returns and pay VAT due was enough. The penalty is at large.
cases.relevance: Simply not declaring income or not filing, if done dishonestly, can be a crime with no statutory maximum sentence. Never advise 'just don't declare it' or leaving out cash or uninvoiced PO jobs.
cases.status: Good law.
cases.note: The URL supplied is R v Stannard [2005] EWCA Crim 2717 (Court of Appeal, Criminal Division, 1 November 2005), which discusses Mavji on cheating the public revenue (checked 24 Nov 2026); the 1986 judgment itself was not opened.
cases.source_note: The link is to R v Stannard [2005] EWCA Crim 2717, which discusses it; the original judgment was not checked.

cases.name: Dosanjh and others v R
cases.principle: Cheating the public revenue is a common-law offence Parliament deliberately preserved; its penalty is at large and courts are not limited by the statutory maxima for fraudulent evasion offences. It is reserved for the most serious revenue frauds; a 13-year sentence (reduced from 15) was imposed for a fraud of about £39m.
cases.relevance: Shows how seriously evasion is treated and gives the basis for firm refusals, and for explaining consequences, when a user asks for help hiding income or faking expenses.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: HMRC v Marc Gunnarsson
cases.principle: Entitlement to a statutory payment (here a SEISS grant) depends only on the statutory conditions, not on HMRC guidance or the claimant's honest belief, and someone trading through their own company is not self-employed. The Tribunal warned that citing non-existent, AI-generated decisions may lead to sanctions ([108]-[115]).
cases.relevance: Guidance is not law, so the assistant must check the legislation, and honest misunderstanding creates no entitlement. A direct warning that an AI assistant must never invent or misquote authorities and should link only to judgments it has verified.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Hill and McCracken v HMRC
cases.principle: Relying on an adviser is a reasonable excuse only if the reliance was objectively reasonable; accepting advice without checking it or asking questions, with no reasonable basis for believing it right, is not enough (applying Perrin) ([52]-[53]).
cases.relevance: If the user relies on this app's AI or an accountant, an excuse for an error or late filing stands only if that reliance was objectively reasonable. The assistant should cite official sources, flag uncertainty and suggest checks.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: HMRC v HFFX LLP; Atkins and others v HMRC
cases.principle: Money paid to members under a discretionary deferral plan designed to reduce tax was still taxable as miscellaneous income from a 'source' under ITTOIA s687, even without an absolute entitlement; the partnership rule in s850 requires a contractual right to the profits during the period.
cases.relevance: Plans to defer or reroute earnings to cut tax tend to fail because catch-all charges still tax the income; this supports using only reliefs, timing and method choices, never avoidance arrangements.
cases.status: Good law.

cases.name: Mainpay Ltd v HMRC
cases.principle: An umbrella company's relationship with its temporary workers was not an overarching contract of employment, so there was no single continuing employment to support its tax-free travel and subsistence treatment; the FTT was entitled to find the loss of tax careless, extending the discovery time limit.
cases.relevance: If the user ever takes PAYE work through an umbrella company or agency, 'tax-free expenses' offers carry real risk. As a genuine sole trader, travel to venues is judged instead under the ITTOIA s34 rules.
cases.status: Good law as at the 10 October 2025 judgment (appeal dismissed).
cases.note: Whether permission to appeal to the Supreme Court was sought was not checked.

cases.name: Medpro Healthcare Ltd v HMRC
cases.court: Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber), Marcus Smith J and Judge Cannan; 30 July 2025
cases.principle: When deciding whether to admit a late appeal, the FTT must actually carry out the Martland three-stage balancing exercise and give adequate reasons; the UT allowed the appeal on that basis and remitted the case to a differently constituted FTT.
cases.relevance: A late appeal against an HMRC decision or penalty is possible but not automatic: the length of and reasons for delay matter, so flag appeal deadlines early.
cases.status: Partly reversed. Its further holding, on Marcus Smith J's casting vote, that the Martland/Katib extra weight for time limits fetters the FTT's discretion under VATA s83G(6) was reversed by the Court of Appeal in HMRC v MedPro [2026] EWCA Civ 14. The remittal holding (grounds 1-3) stands.

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 ss5 and 34: charge on trade profits; expenses not wholly and exclusively for the trade
legislation.citation: Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005, ss5, 34(1)-(2)
legislation.what_it_does: s5 charges income tax on the profits of a trade, profession or vocation. s34(1)(a) bars any deduction for an expense not incurred wholly and exclusively for the trade, and s34(1)(b) bars losses not connected with or arising out of the trade. s34(2) allows a deduction for any identifiable part or identifiable proportion of a mixed expense that is incurred wholly and exclusively for the trade.
