legislation.relevance: The core test for every expense. s34(2) is the basis for claiming the business share of a phone, broadband, a car's running costs or a hotel bill that includes a private night; it does not rescue an expense whose single purpose is itself mixed (everyday clothing, ordinary lunches: Mallalieu, Caillebotte). The trader must prove the identifiable proportion (Healy FTT 2015).
legislation.status: Law (in force). legislation.gov.uk text up to date to 22-23 Nov 2026; the only pending effect (2026 asc 7 Sch 2 para 370(b)) amends s168, not these sections.

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 s33: capital expenditure (accruals/GAAP basis only)
legislation.citation: Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005, s33
legislation.what_it_does: No deduction is allowed for items of a capital nature in calculating trade profits; relief for capital spending on plant and machinery comes instead through capital allowances (CAA 2001), for example the Annual Investment Allowance.
legislation.relevance: Applies only if the trader has elected out of the cash basis under s25C: s32A(1) disapplies s33 on the cash basis, where s33A applies instead. On the accruals basis, buying lighting, audio or rigging kit or a laptop is capital, relieved by capital allowances.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 s24A: cash basis is the default from 2024-25
legislation.citation: ITTOIA 2005 s24A (inserted by FA 2024 Sch 10 paras 2 and 47); read with s33A and CAA 2001 s1A
legislation.what_it_does: From 2024-25, an individual's (or all-individual partnership's) trade profits must be calculated on the cash basis (receipts received less expenses paid) unless the trade is an excluded trade under s25B or a GAAP election under s25C has effect. ss27, 28 and 30 do not apply where the cash basis applies. With s33A and CAA 2001 s1A, capital spending is generally deductible when paid (with exclusions such as cars, land, non-depreciating assets and training), and capital allowances remain only for cars.
legislation.relevance: For 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27 the freelancer is on the cash basis unless they opted out. For 2023-24 the old rules applied: the cash basis needed an election under the former s25A, was available only up to £150,000 of receipts (BIM70010), capped interest at £500, and barred sideways loss relief (ITA s74E). Invoices unpaid at 5 April are taxed when paid, a legitimate timing difference. Check which basis applied in each year before advising on equipment, interest or losses.
legislation.status: Law: in force from 6 April 2024 for 2024-25 and later years; legislation.gov.uk text up to date to 23 Nov 2026.

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 ss25B-25C: excluded trades, and election to use GAAP instead of the cash basis
legislation.citation: ITTOIA 2005 ss25B and 25C (inserted by FA 2024 Sch 10 paras 5, 11, 47)
legislation.what_it_does: s25C lets a trader of a non-excluded trade elect for profits to be calculated under GAAP (accruals). The election has effect for that tax year and later years until revoked by electing back to the cash basis or until the trade becomes excluded (s25C(3)). s25B lists the excluded trades (Conditions A-G): firms with a non-individual partner, LLPs, herd basis, profit averaging, BPRA within 7 years, mineral extraction, and R&D allowance assets still owned.
legislation.relevance: Choosing between methods is a legitimate way to reduce tax. The cash basis taxes money only when received (helps when clients pay late) and lets most equipment be expensed at once under s33A; the accruals basis gives bad-debt relief (s35) and capital allowances. A freelance technician is not an excluded trade. HMRC says the choice is made on the SA return by stating that traditional accounting was used; switching can create adjustments.
legislation.status: Law: in force from 6 April 2024; no amendments to ss25B or 25C on legislation.gov.uk as of 23 Nov 2026.

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 s32A: rules that do not apply on the cash basis (including the car-hire restriction)
legislation.what_it_does: On the cash basis, s33 (capital), s35 (bad debts), ss36-37 (unpaid remuneration), s43 and ss48-50B (car-hire restriction) do not apply; s33A (cash-basis capital rule) applies instead.
legislation.relevance: On the cash basis the 15% disallowance for hiring high-emission cars does not apply, so the full business proportion of hire-car charges is deductible. Bad-debt relief is irrelevant because unpaid invoices are never taxed.
legislation.status: Law (in force, as amended by FA 2024).

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 s33A: cash basis — which capital expenditure is deductible
legislation.citation: ITTOIA 2005 s33A (substituted by F(No 2)A 2017 Sch 2 para 2)
legislation.what_it_does: On the cash basis, capital expenditure is deductible in the year it is paid, except spending on: acquiring or disposing of a business; education or training; providing, altering or disposing of a non-depreciating asset (one not expected to end its useful life or lose 90% of its value within 20 years), an asset not acquired for continuing use in the trade, a car, land (with a fixtures carve-out), non-qualifying intangibles or financial assets.
legislation.relevance: The main timing lever: cables, lighting, audio and comms kit, tools, flight cases, laptops and vans are deducted in the year paid. Cars are excluded but keep capital allowances (CAA 2001 s1A(4)) if the mileage rate has not been used (BIM72035). Capital training (see Dass) is barred.
legislation.status: Law (in force; current text effective 2017-18 onward; applies to the default cash basis from 2024-25).

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 s96A: capital receipts under, or after leaving, the cash basis
legislation.what_it_does: If capital spending on an asset was deducted on the cash basis, sale proceeds, insurance or compensation, or a refund of that spending are taxed as trading receipts (also after leaving the cash basis where the spending would not have qualified for capital allowances). The receipt is reduced proportionately if only part of the cost was deducted, and not taxed twice where a capital allowances disposal value covers it. Ceasing to use the asset in the trade is a disposal at market value; a material increase in private use is a disposal of the increase in the private-use share of market value (s96A(5)-(6)).
legislation.relevance: Selling used equipment expensed under s33A creates taxable income, as do insurance pay-outs for stolen or damaged kit and taking kit into private use. Flag whenever the user sells or retires kit.
legislation.status: Law (in force; text up to date to 22 Nov 2026; FA 2024 Sch 10 para 21 substitutions apply from 2024-25).

legislation.name: CAA 2001 s1A: no capital allowances on the cash basis, except for cars
legislation.what_it_does: For a chargeable period in which profits are on the cash basis, no capital allowances or balancing charges arise, except for cars (s1A(4)-(5)); transitional rules cover assets bought before entering the cash basis.
legislation.relevance: On the cash basis, equipment is relieved as an expense (s33A), not by capital allowances. The trader's own car is the exception: either capital allowances plus the business share of actual running costs, or the s94D-94F mileage rate, but not both.
legislation.status: Law (in force; amended by FA 2024 Sch 10 para 39 for 2024-25 onward).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2024 s16 and Schedule 10: cash basis made the default; interest cap and loss restriction removed
legislation.citation: Finance Act 2024 (c. 3), s16 and Sch 10 (in particular paras 2, 4-8, 11, 16, 47-50); Royal Assent 22 February 2024
legislation.what_it_does: From 2024-25 makes the cash basis the default for trading profits (new ITTOIA s24A, para 2), except for excluded trades (s25B, para 11) and traders electing for GAAP (s25C, para 5). Repeals the old opt-in election in s25A (para 4) and the turnover entry and exit limits (ss31A, 31B, 31D by para 6; s31C by para 16). Removes the loan-interest restriction: s51A (para 7(a)) and the £500 interest-plus-finance-costs allowance in s57B (para 7(b)). Repeals ITA 2007 s74E (para 8(a)), which had denied sideways relief (ss64, 72) and TCGA s261B relief for cash-basis losses.
legislation.relevance: From 2024-25, business loan or credit-card interest and finance costs (a van loan, equipment finance) are deductible on the cash basis without the £500 limit, and cash-basis losses (for example from a heavy equipment year) can be set sideways against other income. Neither was possible in 2023-24 under the old cash basis.
legislation.status: Law: in force for 2024-25 and later tax years (Sch 10 para 47; transitional rules paras 48-50).

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 ss94D-94G: simplified expenses — fixed-rate mileage for vehicles
legislation.citation: ITTOIA 2005 ss94D, 94E, 94F, 94G (Part 2 Ch 5A, inserted by FA 2013 Sch 5); s94F(2)-(3) amended by Taxation (Energy and Vehicles) Act 2026 s2; CAA 2001 s38ZA
legislation.what_it_does: Instead of the actual costs of acquiring, owning, hiring, leasing or using a car, goods vehicle or motorcycle, a trader may deduct a fixed amount per business mile (s94D). Once used for a vehicle, the method must continue for as long as that vehicle is used in the trade, and no other deduction or capital allowance is given for its acquisition, hire or running costs (s94D(4), CAA s38ZA). A vehicle is excluded if capital allowances have ever been claimed on it, or if it is a van or motorcycle whose cost was deducted on the cash basis (s94E). Rates (s94F): car or goods vehicle 45p per mile for the first 10,000 business miles and 25p after for 2023-24 to 2025-26; 55p and 25p from 2026-27; motorcycle 24p.
legislation.relevance: Often the most valuable claim for the freelancer's own car: 10,000 business miles is worth £5,500 in 2026-27 against £4,500 in 2023-24 to 2025-26. Only business journeys or identifiable business parts count, not ordinary commuting. Parking, tolls and congestion charges are claimed on top (BIM75005). Compare mileage with actual costs plus capital allowances before the first claim for each vehicle, because the choice is locked. Hire cars are separate vehicles: claim the actual hire charge plus fuel.
legislation.status: Law (in force). The 55p first-10,000-mile rate applies from 2026-27 (TEVA 2026 s2). The rise to 35p above 10,000 miles from 6 April 2027 is announced, not law.

legislation.name: Taxation (Energy and Vehicles) Act 2026 s2: mileage rates raised from 45p to 55p
legislation.citation: Taxation (Energy and Vehicles) Act 2026 (c. 26), s2; Royal Assent 15 July 2026
legislation.what_it_does: Substitutes 55p for 45p in ITEPA 2003 s230(2) (employee approved mileage allowance payments) and ITTOIA 2005 s94F(2)-(3) (self-employed simplified mileage), with effect for 2026-27 and later tax years; in force at Royal Assent. The over-10,000-mile rate stays at 25p in law, and motorcycles at 24p.
legislation.relevance: Confirms the 55p rate for 2026-27 business mileage, including miles logged before the June 2026 announcement; 2023-24 to 2025-26 stay at 45p. The rate is per tax year, so a non-tax-year accounting period applies the rate for the tax year being computed (BIM75005 worked examples).
legislation.status: Law: in force at Royal Assent (15 July 2026), with effect for 2026-27 and later tax years.

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 s94H (and s94I): simplified expenses — use of home flat rate
legislation.what_it_does: Instead of apportioning actual household running costs, a trader may deduct a flat monthly amount based on hours spent wholly and exclusively on business work at home: £10 for 25-50 hours, £18 for 51-100 hours, £26 for 101 or more; hours are counted once where several people work at the same time. Not available to firms with a non-individual partner (s94C). s94I gives a separate fixed-rate private-use adjustment where business premises are also the trader's home (for example a B&B).
legislation.relevance: Suits a technician doing admin, quotes, invoicing and show prep at home, though few home hours make it small (30 hours a month gives £120 a year). Compare each year with actual-cost apportionment (BIM47820). Phone, broadband and an identifiable business share of fixed costs such as council tax can be claimed on top (BIM75010). A yearly choice, not a lock-in.
legislation.status: Law (in force for 2023-24 to 2026-27; rates unchanged since FA 2013).

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 s57A: traders' food and drink when travelling (itinerant trades and occasional journeys)
legislation.citation: ITTOIA 2005 s57A (inserted by the Enactment of Extra-Statutory Concessions Order 2009, SI 2009/730, arts 1(1) and 3)
legislation.what_it_does: Allows a deduction for reasonable food or drink the trader consumes at, or while travelling to, a place visited for the trade if (Condition A) the travel to that place is deductible, or would be if the trader paid for it, and (Condition B) the trade is itinerant by nature, or the trader goes there no more than occasionally and the trip is outside any normal pattern of travel (or there is no such pattern).
legislation.relevance: The statutory exception to Caillebotte v Quinn: meals on journeys to a one-off venue, or throughout a genuinely itinerant touring pattern, can be deductible; daily lunches at a regular venue, a long single-site engagement, or a commute are not. Meals taken with a business overnight stay are separately allowed under HMRC practice (BIM37670, BIM47705). Keep receipts and amounts reasonable.
legislation.status: Law: in force for 2009-10 and later tax years; unamended as of 23 Nov 2026.

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 s45 (with ss46-47): business entertainment and gifts disallowed
legislation.what_it_does: No deduction is allowed for expenses of providing entertainment (including hospitality of any kind) or gifts, together with incidental costs, subject to the exceptions in s46 (for example staff entertainment) and s47 (certain gifts).
legislation.relevance: Buying drinks or meals for clients, production managers or crew is not deductible, even if done to win work; this overrides the result in Bentleys v Beeson. Do not suggest client hospitality as a deduction.
legislation.status: Law (in force; text up to date to 22 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 ss48-50A: 15% car-hire restriction (accruals basis only) and short-term hire exception
legislation.citation: ITTOIA 2005 ss48, 49, 50A (as amended or inserted by FA 2009 Sch 11 paras 36-39); CAA 2001 s104AA; HMRC BIM47714, BIM47750
legislation.what_it_does: For a trader on the accruals basis, the deduction for hiring a car (not a van or motorcycle) is cut by 15% unless the car is electric, was first registered before 1 March 2001, is a qualifying hire car (hire-purchase-type deal or long funding lease), or emits no more than 50g/km CO2 (CAA s104AA; from 6 April 2021). s50A disapplies the cut where the car is made available for no more than 45 consecutive days, counting linked hires of the same car separated by 14 days or less (even with different hire companies), unless arranged mainly to avoid the rule or tax. On the cash basis ss48-50B do not apply at all (s32A).
legislation.relevance: Short hire cars for gigs and tours (45 days or less) are fully deductible whatever their emissions, with fuel for business journeys. A long-term lease of a petrol or diesel car on the accruals basis loses 15% of the hire charge. Do not apply the 15% cut to ordinary short gig hires.
legislation.status: Law (in force for hire periods from 6 April 2009; text up to date to 23-24 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 s57: pre-trading expenses
legislation.what_it_does: Expenses incurred for a trade up to 7 years before it starts, which would have been deductible if incurred after the start, are treated as incurred on the first day of trading.
legislation.relevance: Set-up costs paid before formally starting (insurance, website, software, tools, travel to win first clients) are not lost: they are deducted in the first period, subject to the normal capital and wholly-and-exclusively rules. Capital items fall under CAA s12 (treated as bought on day one) or, on the cash basis, s33A.
legislation.status: Law (in force; up to date to 23 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: ITEPA 2003 s339: workplace, temporary workplace and the 24-month rule (employees only)
legislation.what_it_does: For employees only, travel to a 'temporary workplace' (attended for a task of limited duration or some other temporary purpose) is relievable; a place stops being temporary where continuous work there lasts, or is expected to last, more than 24 months (s339(5)).
legislation.relevance: The 24-month rule does not apply to a self-employed trader; never use it to justify a freelancer's long-engagement travel, where the trading tests (s34, Samadian, Healy) apply. If the crew member is engaged on PAYE for a production, that engagement falls under the ITEPA rules.
legislation.status: Law (in force; no pending amendments as of 23 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: ITEPA 2003 s4: meaning of 'employment'
legislation.what_it_does: Gives a partial definition: 'employment' includes employment under a contract of service, under a contract of apprenticeship, and in Crown service. 'Contract of service' is not defined, so whether a freelancer is employed on an engagement is decided by the common-law tests (Ready Mixed Concrete, Hall v Lorimer, HMRC v PGMOL [2024] UKSC 29). Other rules can treat income as employment income: s5 (offices), ss44-47 (agency workers) and Part 2 Chs 8 and 10 (IR35/off-payroll).
legislation.relevance: Status is a matter of case law and facts, with no election: the user cannot choose to be self-employed. Legal tax planning means getting the status right and then claiming the reliefs that status allows.
legislation.status: Law (in force, unamended).

legislation.name: ITEPA 2003 s336: employee expenses — the general rule
legislation.what_it_does: An employee can deduct an amount they are obliged to incur and pay as holder of the employment that is incurred wholly, exclusively and necessarily in performing the duties. Travel is excluded from s336 and dealt with by ss337-342. It covers employment income only; trading profits fall under ITTOIA s34 ('wholly and exclusively', with no 'necessarily' test).
legislation.relevance: If a booking is employment (for example the engager puts the user on PAYE), costs for that booking fall under this stricter rule; do not apply the trading test to them.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: ITEPA 2003 Part 2 Ch 7, ss44-47: agency workers
legislation.what_it_does: Where a worker personally provides services (other than excluded services) to a client under or because of a contract between the client (or a connected person) and a third-party agency, the worker is treated as employed by the agency and all their pay for those services is employment income (s44(1), (3)), unless it is shown that how the work is done is not subject to, or to the right of, supervision, direction or control by any person (s44(2)). Excluded services (s47(2)): work as an actor, singer, musician or other entertainer or model, and work done wholly at home or at premises the client does not control and the work does not require.
legislation.relevance: Matters when the user is booked through a crewing agency rather than directly by a production company: the agency must operate PAYE unless there is no supervision, direction or control. Technical crew are not 'entertainers', and the premises exclusion does not apply where the job requires working at the venue. HMRC guidance at ESM2000 onward; NIC equivalent in SI 1978/1689.
legislation.status: Law (in force as amended; s44 substituted by FA 2014 from 6 April 2014; FA 2026 s24(4) removed the fraudulent-document rule in s44(4)(b) and (6) for payments from 6 April 2026; core rules unchanged).

legislation.name: Social Security (Categorisation of Earners) Regulations 1978, Sch 1 Pt I para 2: agency workers for NIC
legislation.what_it_does: Treats a worker as an employed earner for Class 1 NIC if they personally provide services to an end client under, or because of, a contract between that client and an agency and are paid for them, unless (a) all the work is done at home or at premises the client does not control or manage (and the work does not require being there), (b) the worker is an actor, singer, musician, other entertainer or model, or (c) nobody supervises, directs or controls (or has the right to control) how the services are provided.
legislation.relevance: The NIC counterpart of ITEPA s44 for crewing-agency bookings; technicians are not entertainers, so that exclusion does not help them.
legislation.status: Law (para 2 substituted from 6 April 2014 by SI 2014/635; no outstanding effects).

legislation.name: ITEPA 2003 Part 2 Ch 8 (ss48-61) and SI 2000/727 reg 6: IR35 for small clients
legislation.citation: ITEPA 2003 ss48-61 (esp. s49); Social Security Contributions (Intermediaries) Regulations 2000 (SI 2000/727) reg 6
legislation.what_it_does: If a worker personally provides services to a client through an intermediary such as their own company, and would have been the client's employee or office-holder if engaged directly, the intermediary is treated as paying a deemed employment payment at the end of the tax year (s50) and is the secondary contributor for Class 1 NIC on it (SI 2000/727 reg 6). From 6 April 2021 this applies only where the client is not a public authority and is small (Companies Act test, ss60A-60G) or has no UK connection (s60I); otherwise Chapter 10 applies.
legislation.relevance: Does not apply to the user as a sole trader engaged directly. It would apply if they incorporated and worked for small production companies; their company would then judge status using the same case law.
legislation.status: Law (in force; amended by FA 2020 Sch 1 and SI 2020/1220 from 6 April 2021).

legislation.name: ITEPA 2003 Part 2 Ch 10 (ss61K-61X): off-payroll working for public authorities and medium or large clients
legislation.what_it_does: Applies where a worker supplies services through an intermediary (usually their own company, with a material interest over 5%) to a public authority, or a medium or large client with a UK connection, and would be the client's employee if engaged directly (s61M). The fee-payer (the party just above the intermediary, or the client if it has given no valid status determination statement) must deduct PAYE and NIC on deemed employment income (ss61N, 61Q). The client must give a reasoned status determination statement reached with reasonable care (s61NA); if disputed before the final payment, it has 45 days to confirm or revise it, or it takes on the fee-payer's liability (s61T).
legislation.relevance: Applies only if the user works through their own company for medium or large production companies or broadcasters; not to current sole-trader engagements. Client size thresholds: ESM10006A.
legislation.status: Law (in force: public sector from 6 April 2017; medium and large private-sector clients from 6 April 2021; text up to date to 23 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2024 s17 (ITEPA s688AB) and SI 2024/355: off-payroll double-tax offset
legislation.citation: FA 2024 s17; ITEPA 2003 s688AB; Income Tax (Pay As You Earn) (Amendment) (No. 2) Regulations 2024 (SI 2024/355)
legislation.what_it_does: Where a deemed employer owes PAYE because it is treated as making a deemed direct payment under ITEPA s61N(3) (other than s61WA fraud cases), HMRC may direct that income tax or corporation tax already paid on the same income is treated as recovered from the worker, reducing the deemed employer's liability; the worker then cannot reclaim or set off that tax. It applies to deemed direct payments from 6 April 2017 where the trigger event (a reg 80 determination, letter of offer or recovery notice) is on or after 6 April 2024; the payee can appeal within 30 days (PAYE regs 72GA-72GC).
legislation.relevance: Relevant only if the user works through a company with medium or large clients; it means a wrong determination is no longer taxed twice.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: ITEPA 2003 Part 2 Ch 11 (ss61Y-61Z2), inserted by Finance Act 2026 s24: umbrella company PAYE joint and several liability
legislation.what_it_does: For payments from 6 April 2026, each 'relevant party' is jointly and severally liable with an umbrella company for PAYE on qualifying umbrella company payments (s61Y(2)), unless the worker has a material interest (over 5%) in it. The relevant party is normally the person contracting with the client (usually the agency); the client is liable instead where it contracts directly with the umbrella, or the agency is connected with the umbrella or is non-UK resident; if both are non-resident, the UK-resident person closest to the client in the chain (s61Z). Purported umbrella companies are caught too, and the worker is treated as employed by them (s61Z1).
legislation.relevance: A freelancer invoicing production companies directly as a sole trader is outside this. If engaged through an agency and umbrella, the user is the umbrella's employee for that work (PAYE income on the employment pages, no trading deductions), so keep umbrella payslips out of trading turnover. Non-compliant 'enhanced pay' umbrella offers are avoidance (Spotlights 60 and 71).
legislation.status: Law (in force for payments on or after 6 April 2026).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s7: notice of chargeability
legislation.what_it_does: A person chargeable to income tax who has not received a notice to file must tell HMRC within 6 months after the end of the tax year (by 5 October).
legislation.relevance: Applies on starting self-employment or a new income source. Failure triggers FA 2008 Sch 41 penalties and the 20-year assessment limit (s36(1A)(b)).
legislation.status: Law (in force as amended; some FA 2017 Sch 14 MTD wording changes listed as outstanding).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s8: personal return and filing dates
legislation.what_it_does: A return for year 1 is due by 31 October in year 2 on paper or by 31 January in year 2 online. If the notice to file is given after 31 July but by 31 October of year 2, a paper return is due within 3 months of the notice (online still 31 January); if given after 31 October, any return is due within 3 months of the notice.
legislation.relevance: Drives the calendar: the 2025-26 online return is due 31 January 2027 (paper was 31 October 2026); the 2026-27 return is due 31 January 2028.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s9ZA: taxpayer amendment of return
legislation.what_it_does: A taxpayer may amend their return by notice to HMRC, but not more than 12 months after the filing date (normally 31 January of year 2).
legislation.relevance: The simplest legal way to add missed expenses or capital allowances: the 2024-25 return can be amended until 31 January 2027. The 2023-24 window closed on 31 January 2026, so only overpayment relief (Sch 1AB, with exclusions) remains for that year.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s9A: enquiry window
legislation.what_it_does: HMRC can open an enquiry within 12 months after delivery of an on-time return; for a late or amended return the window runs to the quarter day (31 Jan, 30 Apr, 31 Jul, 31 Oct) after the first anniversary of delivery or amendment. Only one enquiry is allowed per return, apart from enquiries into amendments.
legislation.relevance: Filing early and on time closes the enquiry window soonest (Hayes); after that HMRC need a valid discovery under s29.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s12B: duty to keep records
legislation.what_it_does: A trader must keep records needed for a correct and complete return, including all amounts received and spent and what they were for, until the 5th anniversary of the 31 January after the tax year, or later while an enquiry is open or possible. Records may be preserved in any form (s12B(4)), with some exceptions. Penalty for failure: up to £3,000 per year (s12B(5)).
legislation.relevance: 2023-24 records must be kept until at least 31 January 2030. Digital copies of receipts, hotel folios and POs satisfy s12B(4), and good records support expense claims in an enquiry.
legislation.status: Law (in force, as amended).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s29: discovery assessments
legislation.what_it_does: HMRC may assess if an officer discovers that tax ought to have been assessed, that an assessment is insufficient, or that relief is excessive. Where a return was filed, they may do so only if the loss was brought about carelessly or deliberately by the taxpayer or someone acting for them (s29(4)), or a hypothetical officer could not reasonably have been aware of it from the information made available (s29(5)-(6)). Returns made in line with prevailing practice are protected (s29(2)). Since FA 2022 s97, s29(1)(a) covers 'an amount of income tax or capital gains tax'.
legislation.relevance: After the enquiry window closes this is HMRC's only route. Full disclosure in the return plus reasonable care gives real finality (Langham v Veltema); HMRC bear the burden of proving the conditions (Burgess).
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s34: ordinary 4-year time limit
legislation.what_it_does: An assessment (other than a self-assessment) may be made no more than 4 years after the end of the tax year; a time-limit objection can only be raised on appeal.
legislation.relevance: Where the freelancer took reasonable care, 2022-23 cannot be assessed after 5 April 2027 and 2023-24 after 5 April 2028.
legislation.status: Law (in force; text up to date to 23 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s36: extended time limits (careless, deliberate, failure to notify)
legislation.what_it_does: The time limit is 6 years for a loss of tax brought about carelessly, and 20 years for one brought about deliberately, through failure to notify under s7, or in certain avoidance cases. Losses brought about by someone acting on the person's behalf count (s36(1B)). Reliefs the taxpayer would have been entitled to must be given in the late assessment if claimed (s36(3)).
legislation.relevance: Reasonable care keeps exposure to 4 years. In any late assessment, ask for unclaimed reliefs (missed expenses or allowances) to be set off under s36(3).
legislation.status: Law (in force; no outstanding effects; text up to date to 23 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s43 and Schedule 1AB: claims and overpayment relief
legislation.what_it_does: s43(1): an income tax or CGT claim must be made within 4 years after the end of the tax year it relates to, unless another provision sets a different period. Sch 1AB: a person who has paid, or been assessed for, tax that was not due can claim repayment or discharge within 4 years after the end of the relevant tax year (para 3), but not in a return. HMRC need not give relief in Cases A-H (para 2): A, a mistake in or failure to make a claim, election or notice (including capital allowances pooling and disposal values); B, relief still obtainable by other steps such as an s9ZA amendment; C, such steps were available only for a period now expired and the claimant knew or ought to have known; D-E, grounds raised or that could have been raised in an appeal; F, payments under enforcement or settlements; G-H, calculations under prevailing practice.
legislation.relevance: A legal way to recover missed business expenses, for example 2022-23 until 5 April 2027. But missed capital allowance claims generally must be made by amending the return within the s9ZA window, so warn early. Reasonable excuse does not extend these limits (Raftopoulou).
legislation.status: Law (in force as amended; text up to date to 23-24 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 ss31, 31A and 49: appeals and late appeals
legislation.what_it_does: An appeal lies against enquiry amendments, closure-notice conclusions and assessments other than self-assessments (s31). Notice must be in writing to HMRC within 30 days (s31A). A late appeal needs HMRC's agreement, which HMRC must give if there was a reasonable excuse and no unreasonable delay, or the tribunal's permission (s49), applying Martland and MedPro.
legislation.relevance: The app should calendar 30 days from any HMRC decision or closure notice.
legislation.status: Law (in force; no outstanding changes).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s118(2), (5)-(7): reasonable-excuse deeming; meaning of careless and deliberate
legislation.what_it_does: Within TMA only, a person is treated as not having failed to meet a time limit if they acted within extra time allowed, or had a reasonable excuse and acted without unreasonable delay once it ended (s118(2)); this does not extend deadlines for optional claims (Raftopoulou) and does not govern Sch 55/56 penalties, which have their own excuse rules. A loss of tax is brought about carelessly if the person fails to take reasonable care to avoid it (s118(5)); an inaccuracy the person later discovers but does not take reasonable steps to tell HMRC about is treated as careless (s118(6)); deliberate is defined in s118(7).
legislation.relevance: The definition of careless governs the 6-year limit. If the freelancer later spots an error, telling HMRC promptly avoids it being treated as careless.
legislation.status: Law (in force; (5)-(7) inserted by FA 2008 Sch 39 from 1 April 2010; text up to date to 23 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 Schedule A1 paras 11-12: MTD digital records and penalty
legislation.citation: TMA 1970 Sch A1 paras 11-12 (as amended by FA 2026 ss256-258)
legislation.what_it_does: HMRC may require relevant persons (sole traders and landlords) to keep and preserve specified business records electronically, in addition to s12B; failure attracts a penalty of up to £3,000, unless a s12B(5) penalty applies for the same period.
legislation.relevance: If the freelancer is within MTD for Income Tax (qualifying income over £50,000 from April 2026, over £30,000 from April 2027, over £20,000 from April 2028), records must be kept digitally in compatible software.
legislation.status: Law: in force from 1 April 2026; FA 2026 ss256-258 amended parts of it; operative regulations SI 2026/336.

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s59A: payments on account and the claim to reduce them (SA303)
legislation.citation: Taxes Management Act 1970, s59A(3), (4) and (6); HMRC form SA303
legislation.what_it_does: Two payments on account, each 50% of the previous year's liability not deducted at source, are due on 31 January and 31 July; they are not required if last year's liability was under £1,000 or over 80% was collected at source (GOV.UK). A taxpayer who believes the current year's liability will be lower can claim, giving grounds, to reduce them or set them to nil, by 31 January after the tax year, online or on SA303. A fraudulent or negligent incorrect statement in the claim attracts a penalty up to the shortfall (s59A(6)), and interest runs on any underpayment.
legislation.relevance: A legal cash-flow tool after a lower-profit year, or where new pension contributions or losses cut the bill. Base any reduction on a reasoned estimate from the books and warn about interest and the s59A(6) penalty if it is too low.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: TMA 1970 s106A (fraudulent evasion of income tax) and VATA 1994 s72 (fraudulent evasion of VAT)
legislation.citation: TMA 1970 s106A (inserted by TIOPA 2010 Sch 7 para 95); VATA 1994 s72
legislation.what_it_does: TMA s106A makes it an offence to be knowingly concerned in the fraudulent evasion of income tax by oneself or by any other person. VATA s72(1) is the equivalent for VAT, and s72(3) adds an offence of producing false documents or statements with intent to deceive. FA 2024 s32(1) raised the maximum on indictment from 7 to 14 years for offences on or after 22 February 2024; summary penalties are up to 12 months (6 months for earlier offences and in Northern Ireland) and/or a fine for s106A, and up to 6 months and/or the greater of the statutory maximum or three times the VAT for s72.
legislation.relevance: 'Or any other person' makes helping someone else evade a crime too. The assistant must not help the user evade, nor help them help a client, colleague or supplier evade (cash-in-hand invoices, fake receipts, dishonestly splitting invoices to stay under the VAT threshold).
legislation.status: Law (in force; both confirmed up to date to 23 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2007 Schedule 24: penalties for inaccuracies
legislation.what_it_does: A penalty applies for a careless or deliberate inaccuracy causing a potential loss of revenue: for domestic matters 30% careless, 70% deliberate, 100% deliberate and concealed (para 4). Disclosure reduces it, for careless errors to as low as 0% if unprompted or 15% if prompted (para 10). Careless penalties can be suspended for up to 2 years with conditions (para 14); there is a special reduction (para 11). A taxpayer is not liable for an agent's inaccuracy if they took reasonable care (para 18(3)). An error later discovered and not reported is treated as careless (para 3(2)). An inaccuracy based on avoidance arrangements is presumed careless unless reasonable care is shown, and reliance on 'disqualified' advice (from someone involved in the arrangements, or not addressing the person's circumstances) does not count (para 3A).
legislation.relevance: If the freelancer finds an over-claim (for example personal travel booked as business), unprompted disclosure before HMRC contact can cut a careless penalty to nil. Relying on a promoter's or umbrella company's assurance is not reasonable care.
legislation.status: Law (in force as amended; text up to date to 22 Nov 2026; an uncommenced FA 2015 'category 0' change does not affect domestic rates).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2008 Schedule 36: information and inspection powers
legislation.what_it_does: An HMRC officer may by written notice require a taxpayer to provide information or documents reasonably required to check their tax position or (since FA 2021) to collect a tax debt (para 1). Once a return is filed, a notice about that period needs one of Conditions A-E (para 21), chiefly an open enquiry or reason to suspect under-assessment. There is no appeal against a demand for statutory records (para 62) or a tribunal-approved notice (para 29). Penalties: £300 (para 39), then up to £60 a day (para 40), which the tribunal can raise to up to £1,000 a day (para 49A); up to £3,000 per careless or deliberate inaccuracy (para 40A).
legislation.relevance: Respond on time to any information notice. Requests for non-business or non-statutory material, or post-filing notices without an enquiry or reasonable suspicion, can be challenged.
legislation.status: Law (commenced 1 April 2009; para 1 amended by FA 2021 s127; para 21 Condition E added by F(No.2)A 2023).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2008 Schedule 41: failure to notify
legislation.what_it_does: A penalty applies for failing to notify chargeability under TMA s7: 30% non-deliberate, 70% deliberate, 100% deliberate and concealed, of potential lost revenue (para 6). For a non-deliberate failure disclosed unprompted it can fall to 0% if HMRC learn of it within 12 months of the tax first becoming unpaid, otherwise 10% (para 13). Reasonable excuse applies to non-deliberate failures (para 20), and there is agency relief if reasonable care was taken (para 21).
legislation.relevance: Relevant to any new income stream; notifying by 5 October avoids it entirely.
legislation.status: Law (in force as amended; text current to 23-24 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2009 Schedule 55: late filing penalties
legislation.what_it_does: For a late SA return: £100 (para 3); after 3 months, £10 a day for up to 90 days if HMRC decide and give notice (para 4); after 6 months, the greater of 5% of the tax due or £300 (para 5); after 12 months, the greater of 5% or £300, or up to 70% or 100% if information was deliberately withheld (para 6). Special reduction (para 16). Reasonable excuse (para 23) excludes insufficiency of funds unless outside the person's control, and reliance on another person unless reasonable care was taken; the failure must be remedied without unreasonable delay once the excuse ends.
legislation.relevance: Applies to the 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 returns, and to 2026-27 if the freelancer is not MTD-mandated. Even a nil-tax return attracts £100 or more if late (Edwards). For a return 12 months late with little tax due, the fixed penalties total £1,600 (£100 + £900 + £300 + £300).
legislation.status: Law (in force). Replaced for income tax by FA 2021 Sch 24 for MTD digitally obligated persons for 2026-27 (SI 2026/370); extension to all personal SA returns from April 2027 is announced on GOV.UK, but no commencing SI is shown on legislation.gov.uk.

legislation.name: Finance Act 2009 Schedule 56: late payment penalties
legislation.what_it_does: For an SA balancing payment (TMA s59B), 5% of tax unpaid 30 days after the due date, then a further 5% if unpaid 5 months and 11 months after the penalty date (para 3). Payments on account (s59A) are not in the table. Special reduction (para 9); a time-to-pay agreement suspends penalties while kept (para 10); reasonable excuse excludes insufficiency of funds unless outside the person's control (para 16).
legislation.relevance: If the freelancer cannot pay by 31 January, agreeing time to pay before the 30-day point avoids the penalty, though interest still runs. Payments on account carry interest but no Sch 56 penalty.
legislation.status: Law (in force; replaced by FA 2021 Sch 26 for income tax only for eligible volunteers from 2024-25 and MTD-mandated digitally obligated persons from 2026-27).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2021 ss116-118 and Schedules 24-27: new penalty regime
legislation.what_it_does: Sch 24 sets points-based late submission penalties (a £200 penalty when the points threshold is reached and for each later failure; threshold 2 for annual obligations and 4 for quarterly, para 5(9)). Sch 25 covers deliberate withholding of information. Sch 26 sets late payment penalties: a first penalty on tax unpaid at day 15 and day 30, then a daily-accruing second penalty from day 31. Sch 27 makes consequential amendments. Each comes into force on days appointed by Treasury regulations, which may differ by purpose.
legislation.relevance: Replaces Sch 55/56 for the freelancer's personal return from the year they join MTD for Income Tax (and, as announced, for all SA filers from 2027-28). One late return no longer means an automatic £100; points accrue to a threshold before any £200 penalty.
legislation.status: Law, in force only for purposes appointed so far (VAT, ITSA volunteers, MTD digitally obligated persons). Rates raised by SI 2025/589; amended by FA 2026.

legislation.name: Finance Act 2021 (Income Tax and Capital Gains Tax) (Penalties) (Appointed Day: Digitally Obligated Persons) Regulations 2026
legislation.what_it_does: From 1 April 2026, FA 2021 Schs 24-27 apply to 'digitally obligated persons' (those required to make MTD periodic updates in 2026-27) for their personal returns and income tax/CGT payments for 2026-27 and later years; trustees and partnerships are excluded.
legislation.relevance: If the freelancer's 2024-25 qualifying income exceeded £50,000, their 2026-27 return (due 31 January 2028) and payments fall under the points and new late-payment regime.
legislation.status: Law (made 25 March 2026; appointed day 1 April 2026; no amendments listed).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2021 (Increase in Schedule 26 Penalty Percentages) Regulations 2025
legislation.what_it_does: Raises FA 2021 Sch 26 late payment penalties: the first penalty becomes 3% of tax still unpaid after 15 days plus a further 3% of tax still unpaid after 30 days (was 2% + 2%), and the second penalty 10% a year accruing daily on tax unpaid after day 30 (was 4%). It covers failures with a specified date on or after 31 May 2025, but not income tax or CGT for 2024-25 or earlier. Other SA taxpayers stay under FA 2009 Sch 56.
legislation.relevance: These rates apply to the freelancer's 2026-27 payments if MTD-mandated. GOV.UK states rates of 4%/4% (plus 10% a year) for 2027-28, but the instrument for that rise was not located.
legislation.status: Law (in force 31 May 2025).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2026 ss259, 262, 263 and 264: MTD penalty amendments
legislation.what_it_does: s259 makes consequential amendments after s258 moved electronic SA filing into TMA Sch A1 para 9: it redefines the Sch 24 return entries, limits the one-point-a-month cap in para 5(2) to quarterly groups, and omits redundant provisions. s262 lets HMRC cancel a penalty point (any penalty that relied on it is treated as never having had effect), withdraw a late submission penalty assessment, and expire points early by notice; a late return covered by a reasonable excuse is treated as on time for expiry purposes. s263 lets HMRC withdraw a Sch 26 late payment penalty assessment. s264 extends Sch 56 and Sch 26 to tax payable after a further appeal (TMA s56(3)(b)).
legislation.relevance: Gives legal routes to ask HMRC to cancel a wrongly awarded point or withdraw a late payment penalty, alongside a formal appeal.
legislation.status: Law (enacted 18 March 2026; most changes from 1 April 2026).

legislation.name: Income Tax (Digital Obligations) Regulations 2026: MTD for Income Tax thresholds and timetable
legislation.citation: SI 2026/336 (made 23 March 2026, in force 1 April 2026), regs 5, 9, 11-14, 18-27; made under TMA 1970 Sch A1 as amended by FA 2026 ss256-258
legislation.what_it_does: MTD for Income Tax applies from 6 April 2026 if 2024-25 qualifying income exceeded £50,000, from 6 April 2027 if 2025-26 qualifying income exceeded £30,000, and from 6 April 2028 if 2026-27 qualifying income exceeded £20,000 (regs 22, 23, 27). Qualifying income is gross self-employment and property income before deductions (reg 26). Quarterly updates are due 7 August, 7 November, 7 February and 7 May (reg 12). From 2029-30 a person leaves MTD after three consecutive years below the threshold (reg 24). It revokes and replaces SI 2021/1076.
legislation.relevance: Gross invoiced turnover, not profit, decides when MTD starts: over £30,000 in 2025-26 means MTD from April 2027. The app should keep digital records, produce quarterly updates and warn when a threshold is crossed.
legislation.status: Law (in force since 1 April 2026; no amendments recorded). Budget 2026 exemptions are announced, not law.

legislation.name: Taxes and Duties etc (Interest Rate) (Amendment) Regulations 2025: late payment interest at Bank Rate + 4%
legislation.citation: SI 2025/386, reg 2 (amending the Taxes (Interest Rate) Regulations 1989)
legislation.what_it_does: Raises the margin over Bank Rate in the late payment interest formula from 2.5 to 4 percentage points from 6 April 2025, including for income tax self assessment. Repayment interest is unchanged at Bank Rate minus 1%, with a 0.5% floor.
legislation.relevance: Paying late is expensive: 8.00% from 24 November 2026. Interest on late tax and penalties is not deductible (ITTOIA s54). Accurate payments on account, and reduction claims when profits fall, are a legitimate way to manage cash.
legislation.status: Law (made 25 March 2025; in force since 6 April 2025).

legislation.name: CAA 2001 s51A: Annual Investment Allowance
legislation.citation: Capital Allowances Act 2001, s51A (read with ss38A-38B and 51B-51N); £1m limit made permanent by F(No. 2)A 2023 s8
legislation.what_it_does: Gives a 100% allowance on qualifying plant and machinery expenditure, up to £1,000,000 for a 12-month chargeable period (pro-rated for longer or shorter periods), in the period the expenditure is incurred. The trader may claim on all or only part of the expenditure (s51A(7)).
legislation.relevance: On the accruals basis, lighting, sound and rigging kit, tools, flight cases, laptops and vans can be written off in the year of purchase. Because s51A(7) allows a partial claim, the assistant can legally suggest claiming only enough AIA to bring profits down to the top of the personal allowance or basic-rate band, leaving the rest in the pool for writing-down allowances. Not used on the cash basis, where kit is simply deducted when paid (ITTOIA s33A).
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: CAA 2001 ss38B, 12 and 13: AIA exclusions; pre-trading capital spend; assets brought into the business
legislation.citation: Capital Allowances Act 2001, s38B (general exclusions 1-5), s12, s13
legislation.what_it_does: No AIA on (1) expenditure in the chargeable period in which the trade permanently ceases, (2) cars, (4) arrangements changing another person's trade where AIA is the main benefit, or (5) assets within s13 or s14 (acquired for other purposes and later brought into the trade, or gifts). Under s13 such an asset is treated as bought when brought into use, at the lower of market value and cost, and gets writing-down allowances only. Under s12, capital spending before the trade starts is treated as incurred on the first day of trading.
legislation.relevance: Kit the freelancer already owned privately goes into the pool at market value and gets WDAs, not AIA. Kit bought shortly before starting qualifies as bought on day one. A major purchase in the tax year the trade stops gets no AIA or FYA, so timing matters. Cars never get AIA.
legislation.status: Law (in force; up to date to 23 Nov 2026).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2026 s29: 40% first-year allowance for main-rate plant and machinery
legislation.citation: Finance Act 2026 (c. 11), s29, inserting CAA 2001 ss45U and 45V and amending ss46 and 52(3)
legislation.what_it_does: Creates a 40% FYA for expenditure on or after 1 January 2026 on plant or machinery that is unused, not second-hand and not special-rate expenditure. Unlike full expensing (companies only) it is available to sole traders. It is subject to the s46 general exclusions, including cars and the final period of trading, and to the anti-avoidance rule in s45V; some leasing is allowed (s46(4B)). The unrelieved 60% goes to the main pool.
legislation.relevance: For a sole trader spending well under £1m, the 100% AIA covers the same kit and is better, so the FYA rarely changes the answer; one item gets one allowance. Neither applies on the cash basis, where capital allowances are available only for cars, and cars are excluded from this FYA.
legislation.status: Law (in force for expenditure from 1 January 2026; Royal Assent 18 March 2026). A rise to 50% from 1 January 2027 is proposed, not law.

legislation.name: Finance Act 2026 s28: main-pool writing-down allowance cut from 18% to 14%
legislation.citation: Finance Act 2026 (c. 11), s28, amending CAA 2001 s56(1)
legislation.what_it_does: For income tax, the main-rate WDA falls from 18% to 14% for chargeable periods beginning on or after 6 April 2026; a straddling period uses a hybrid rate: 18 x (days before)/(days in period) + 14 x (days on or after)/(days in period), rounded up to 2 decimal places. The special-rate pool stays at 6%.
legislation.relevance: Main pool rate is 18% for 2023-24 to 2025-26 and 14% for a tax-year period in 2026-27; a 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027 period gets 14.06%. Pool balances (cars up to 50g/km, kit where AIA was not claimed) are relieved more slowly, which strengthens the case for claiming AIA in full where it saves higher-rate tax.
legislation.status: Law (in force; Royal Assent 18 March 2026). A further cut to 12% from 6 April 2027 (income tax) is proposed, not law.

legislation.name: CAA 2001 ss104AA, 45D and 205-206: cars — pools, 100% FYA for zero-emission cars, private-use restriction
legislation.citation: CAA 2001 s104AA (main rate car); s45D (zero-emission car FYA) as amended by FA 2026 s30; ss205-206 (partial non-business use)
legislation.what_it_does: A car with CO2 emissions up to 50g/km, an electric car, or a car first registered before 1 March 2001 is a main rate car (main pool at 18%, 14% from 2026-27); other cars go in the special-rate pool at 6%. A new, unused electric or 0g/km car gets a 100% FYA for expenditure incurred by 5 April 2027 for income tax (extended by FA 2026 s30). Cars get no AIA. Where an asset is also used privately, the allowance is reduced to a just and reasonable amount (s205) and the asset goes in its own single-asset pool (s206).
legislation.relevance: The technician's own car gets capital allowances for its business-use share, even on the cash basis (CAA s1A(4)). A new EV bought by 5 April 2027 can be written off 100% (less private use). The alternative is the fixed mileage rate (ITTOIA s94D), and the choice is locked for that vehicle.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: ITA 2007 s64: trade loss relief against general income (sideways relief)
legislation.what_it_does: A trading loss can be deducted from net income of the loss year, the previous year, or both, with the claim stating which year comes first. The claim must be made by the first anniversary of the normal filing date for the loss year (a 2024-25 loss by 31 January 2027). Relief is subject to the commercial test (s66), the restrictions in ss74ZA-74D, the s24A cap, and the income available (s25(4)).
legislation.relevance: A loss year (heavy kit investment, a quiet events year) can produce a refund against PAYE or other income of the same or previous year, but setting it against total income can waste the personal allowance. Model each year choice against carry-forward (s83).
legislation.status: Law (in force). s64(8)(bb), the cross-reference to the repealed cash-basis restriction in s74E, was omitted for 2024-25 onward by FA 2024 Sch 10.

legislation.name: ITA 2007 s66: commercial-basis test for sideways loss relief
legislation.what_it_does: s64 relief is denied unless the trade is carried on throughout the tax year (a) on a commercial basis and (b) with a view to realising profits. A trade carried on so as to give a reasonable expectation of profit is treated as having a view to profit (s66(3)); if the way it is carried on changes during the year, it is judged at the end of the year (s66(5)).
legislation.relevance: Losses from a genuine freelance trade normally pass. A loss-making sideline (kit hire, photography, a hobby-like activity) needs evidence of commercial running (pricing that covers costs, marketing, records, a plan, a route to profit); otherwise only carry-forward is available. See Seven Individuals, Beacon, Macdonald and Wannell v Rothwell.
legislation.status: Law (in force as amended; s66(2) reads 'throughout the tax year' from 2024-25 after FA 2022 Sch 1 para 42).

legislation.name: ITA 2007 ss72-74: early trade losses relief (carry back three years)
legislation.what_it_does: A loss made in the tax year a trade starts, or in any of the next three tax years, can be carried back against net income of the three tax years before the loss year, earliest first (s73). The claim deadline is the first anniversary of the normal filing date for the loss year. The trade must be carried on commercially so that profits could reasonably be expected in that year or within a reasonable time after (s74). Capped by s24A.
legislation.relevance: If the technician moved from employment to freelancing and made a start-up loss (for example buying kit), this can recover PAYE tax paid in earlier employed years, possibly at higher rates.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: ITA 2007 s83: carry-forward trade loss relief
legislation.what_it_does: Any part of a trade loss not otherwise relieved is carried forward and deducted from later profits of the same trade only, before other reliefs against those profits.
legislation.relevance: The fallback when sideways relief would waste the personal allowance or fails s66. Not subject to the s24A cap.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: ITA 2007 s24A: cap on income tax reliefs
legislation.what_it_does: Certain reliefs deducted at Step 2 of the income tax calculation, including s64 sideways relief, s72 early-years relief and s96 post-cessation relief, cannot exceed the greater of £50,000 and 25% of adjusted total income for the year. Relief set against profits of the same trade is outside the cap (s24A(7)(b)).
legislation.relevance: Losses over £50,000 (or 25% of adjusted total income, if higher) used against non-trade income are restricted; apply this when modelling large loss claims.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: ITA 2007 ss89-91: terminal trade loss relief
legislation.what_it_does: When a trade permanently ceases, the terminal loss (defined in s90) can be deducted from profits of the same trade for the final tax year and the three previous tax years.
legislation.relevance: Applies if the freelancer stops trading (for example to take employment or incorporate) with a final-period loss; it recovers tax paid on the trade's earlier profits.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: ITA 2007 ss96-101 and ITTOIA 2005 ss242-257: post-cessation reliefs and receipts
legislation.what_it_does: After a trade permanently ends, payments made within 7 years for remedying defective work, goods or services, damages for them, related legal and insurance costs, and costs of collecting debts counted in profits can be deducted from net income of the year paid (ITA ss96-97), as can debts later proved bad or released (s98). Relief is reduced for expenses deducted but never paid (s99), denied for avoidance (s98A), not doubled (s100), can be used as a CGT loss (s101), is capped by s24A, and must be claimed by the first anniversary of the filing date. Money received after cessation from the old trade is a post-cessation receipt (ITTOIA ss242, 246) unless already counted in profits (s243(2)), so a late-paid invoice is caught on the cash basis (s246(2A)) but not if already taxed as a debtor on accruals (unless bad-debt relief was taken, s248). Deductible costs come off the receipt (s254), and a receipt in a tax year beginning within 6 years after cessation can be taxed as if received on cessation (s257 election).
legislation.relevance: Relevant if the freelancer stops trading or incorporates: a late-paid PO invoice can be carried back to the final trading year, and the costs of chasing a bad debt or a claim over defective work remain relievable.
legislation.status: Law (in force; ITTOIA s254(2A) substituted from 6 April 2024 by FA 2024 Sch 10).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2004 ss188-192: personal pension contributions — relief at source, earnings limit, band extension
legislation.citation: Finance Act 2004, ss188-192 (s190 annual limit for relief; s192 relief at source and s192(4) band extension)
legislation.what_it_does: The member pays net of basic-rate tax and the scheme claims the 20% (s192(1)-(2)). Where the member would pay higher-rate tax, the basic-rate and higher-rate limits are increased by the gross contribution (s192(4)), giving extra relief through Self Assessment. Relief is limited to 100% of relevant UK earnings chargeable for the year, or £3,600 gross if higher (s190).
legislation.relevance: The main legal lever for a profitable sole trader: a contribution of £8,000 net (£10,000 gross) can move £10,000 of profit from 40% to 20% tax. Trading profits count as relevant UK earnings. Contributions count in the tax year they are paid, so timing before 5 April matters. Relief does not reduce Class 4 NIC.
legislation.status: Law (in force; no outstanding effects for ss190 or 192).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2004 ss228, 228A, 228ZA: pension annual allowance, carry forward and taper
legislation.citation: Finance Act 2004, s228 (annual allowance £60,000), s228A (carry forward), s228ZA (taper)
legislation.what_it_does: The annual allowance is £60,000 for 2023-24 onwards (F(No.2)A 2023 s20). Unused allowance from the three previous tax years can be carried forward if the individual was a member of a registered pension scheme in those years, earliest first (s228A). The allowance tapers for adjusted income over £260,000 where threshold income exceeds £200,000, down to £10,000 (s228ZA). The money purchase annual allowance is £10,000.
legislation.relevance: Large one-off contributions in a good year (for example after a long single-client engagement) can use carry forward, provided they stay within the year's relevant UK earnings. Contributions above the allowance trigger an annual allowance charge. Check scheme membership in the carry-forward years.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: ITA 2007 ss35 and 58: personal allowance taper and adjusted net income
legislation.citation: Income Tax Act 2007, ss35, 58; Finance Act 2026 s10 (freeze to 2030-31)
legislation.what_it_does: The personal allowance (£12,570) is reduced by half of adjusted net income above £100,000 (s35). Adjusted net income is net income minus grossed-up Gift Aid donations and minus gross relief-at-source pension contributions (s58, Steps 2-3). FA 2026 s10 freezes the £12,570 allowance and the £37,700 basic-rate limit to 2030-31.
legislation.relevance: Between £100,000 and £125,140 the effective marginal rate is about 60%. Gross pension contributions and Gift Aid reduce adjusted net income pound for pound and restore the allowance, a highly effective legal saving after a big year. The same figure drives the High Income Child Benefit Charge.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: ITA 2007 ss413-430: Gift Aid — basic-rate deduction, band extension and carry-back election
legislation.citation: Income Tax Act 2007, ss413-430 (s414 relief; s424 shortfall charge; s426 carry-back election; s427 charged amount)
legislation.what_it_does: A qualifying donation is treated as made net of basic-rate tax, and the basic and higher rate limits are raised by the grossed-up gift (s414(2)), giving extra relief to higher and additional-rate taxpayers. A donor can elect under s426 to treat a gift as made in the previous year, on or before delivering that year's return and no later than its normal filing date, provided the donor's 'charged amount' for that year (s427: modified net income plus amounts chargeable to CGT) at least equals the grossed-up gifts, including the carried-back gift. If tax charged is less than the basic-rate tax treated as deducted, the shortfall is clawed back (s424).
legislation.relevance: Charitable giving gives higher-rate and personal-allowance-restoration relief (via s58). The s426 carry-back lets a donation made after 5 April, before filing, count against the earlier year where that year had higher income.
legislation.status: Law (in force; no known outstanding effects on ss414, 424, 426, 427).

legislation.name: ITA 2007 ss55A-55E: Marriage Allowance (transferable personal allowance)
legislation.citation: Income Tax Act 2007, ss55A-55E (s55B tax reduction; s55C election)
legislation.what_it_does: A spouse or civil partner can elect to transfer 10% of the personal allowance, rounded up to the next £10 (£1,260), to the other. The recipient gets a tax reduction at the basic rate (up to £252), provided they are not liable at the higher, additional or dividend upper rates and neither claims married couple's allowance. GOV.UK says claims can be backdated to 6 April 2022.
legislation.relevance: Useful if the freelancer is a basic-rate taxpayer and their spouse or civil partner has income below £12,570, or the reverse; a quick, low-risk saving, including backdated years.
legislation.status: Law (in force). Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A (28 Oct 2026) confirms £1,260 for 2026-27 and 2027-28.

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 Part 6A Ch 1 (ss783A-783AR): trading allowance (£1,000) and partial-relief election
legislation.citation: ITTOIA 2005 ss783A-783AR (s783AD amount; s783AE full relief; ss783AH-783AI and s783AM partial relief; ss783AN-783AQ exclusions)
legislation.what_it_does: If relevant trading and miscellaneous receipts do not exceed £1,000 they are not taxed (full relief). If they exceed £1,000, the individual can elect to deduct £1,000 instead of actual expenses (s783AM). Elections are due by the first anniversary of the normal filing date. Relief is excluded where income includes payments from the individual's (or spouse's) employer, a firm in which they are a partner, or a close company in which they are a participator, and in some rent-a-room cases.
legislation.relevance: For the main freelance trade, actual expenses (kit, travel, hotels) will usually exceed £1,000, so the election is rarely beneficial; it is useful for a small side income, and cannot be used on payments from a company the user controls or their own employer.
legislation.status: Law at £1,000 for 2023-24 to 2026-27. The rise to £3,000 from 6 April 2027 is proposed in Finance Bill 2026-27, not law.

legislation.name: Finance Act 2022 Sch 1 Part 6: basis period reform — transition profits, spreading and acceleration
legislation.citation: Finance Act 2022 (c. 3), Sch 1 Part 6 (paras 64-76): para 70 (computation), para 72 (spreading), para 73 (acceleration election, formula A x 5/T in para 73(4)), para 75 (income tax calculation)
legislation.what_it_does: From 2024-25 profits are taxed on a tax-year basis. Transition profits arising in 2023-24, net of overlap relief, are taxed 20% in each of 2023-24 to 2026-27 with the balance in 2027-28, or all at once on earlier cessation (para 72). The trader may elect to bring forward any extra amount into a year, by the first anniversary of that year's normal filing date (para 73); later years are then reduced (BIM81310). Tax on transition profit is computed separately (para 75).
legislation.relevance: Matters only if the freelancer had an accounting date other than 31 March to 5 April before 2024-25. Accelerating transition profit into a low-income year (a loss year, or one with spare personal allowance or basic-rate band) is a legal timing saving. Deadlines: 2024-25 by 31 January 2027 (still open), 2025-26 by 31 January 2028, 2026-27 by 31 January 2029.
legislation.status: Law (in force; Royal Assent 24 February 2022; no outstanding effects on paras 72-73; spreading runs to 2027-28).

legislation.name: VATA 1994 Sch 1 para 1: VAT registration threshold £90,000
legislation.citation: Value Added Tax Act 1994, Sch 1 para 1 (threshold substituted by the Value Added Tax (Increase of Registration Limits) Order 2024, SI 2024/307, from 1 April 2024)
legislation.what_it_does: Registration is compulsory if taxable supplies in the past 12 months exceed £90,000 (rolling month-end test), or if there are reasonable grounds to believe they will exceed £90,000 in the next 30 days alone. The threshold was £85,000 before 1 April 2024; the deregistration threshold is £88,000. Voluntary registration below the threshold is allowed.
legislation.relevance: Day rates on long single-client engagements can cross £90,000 quickly: monitor rolling 12-month turnover monthly and warn before the threshold. Registration is due within 30 days of the end of the month in which it is exceeded. Because clients are VAT-registered production companies, voluntary registration (recovering VAT on kit, hire and hotels) is a legitimate option to model.
legislation.status: Law (£90,000 / £88,000 since 1 April 2024; Budget 2026 Annex A keeps both for 2026-27 and 2027-28).

legislation.name: VAT Regulations 1995 Part VIIA: flat rate scheme eligibility and the limited cost business rule
legislation.citation: VAT Regulations 1995 (SI 1995/2518) regs 55A-55V (reg 55L admission; reg 55M leaving; regs 55A(4) and 55KA limited cost trader, inserted by SI 2017/295)
legislation.what_it_does: A VAT-registered business can join if it expects taxable supplies (excluding VAT) in the next 12 months of no more than £150,000 (reg 55L). It must leave if VAT-inclusive income from taxable and exempt supplies (excluding capital asset sales) exceeded £230,000 in the year to its anniversary, or is expected to exceed £230,000 in the next 30 days, unless HMRC accept next year's income will not exceed £191,500 (reg 55M). A limited cost trader, tested each return period, whose VAT-inclusive spend on 'relevant goods' is below the higher of 2% of flat-rate turnover and £1,000 a year (£250 a quarter) must use 16.5% whatever the sector, or 15.5% in the first year of registration (regs 55A(4), 55KA, 55JB). Relevant goods are goods only, used exclusively for the business, excluding vehicles, parts and fuel (with a transport-sector exception), food and drink, capital goods, goods for resale, leasing or hire (unless that is the main activity) and gifts.
legislation.relevance: A labour-heavy events technician will usually be a limited cost trader, and 16.5% of VAT-inclusive turnover is almost all of the 20% VAT charged, so the FRS usually gives little or no benefit over standard accounting. Model both before recommending it.
legislation.status: Law (in force; SI 2017/295 from 1 April 2017; no outstanding effects on regs 55A, 55KA, 55L, 55M).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2013 Part 5 (ss206-215) and Schs 43-43D: General Anti-Abuse Rule (GAAR) and GAAR Advisory Panel
legislation.what_it_does: Counteracts tax advantages from 'tax arrangements' (where a main purpose is a tax advantage) that are 'abusive', meaning they cannot reasonably be regarded as a reasonable course of action in relation to the relevant provisions (the double reasonableness test, s207(2)). Factors include consistency with policy, contrived or abnormal steps and exploiting shortcomings; indicators of abuse include income for tax purposes significantly less than economic income, and deductions or losses significantly greater than the economic amount (s207(4)). Counteraction must be just and reasonable (s209). Courts must take into account HMRC GAAR guidance approved by the independent GAAR Advisory Panel, and the Panel's opinions (s211).
legislation.relevance: The statutory line the assistant must not cross. Ordinary choices Parliament provides (allowances, method elections, timing of real transactions) are outside it. It covers income tax and CGT (s206(3)) and NICs (via NICA 2014); VAT is not in the s206(3) list.
legislation.status: Law (in force for tax arrangements entered into on or after 17 July 2013).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2013 s212A: GAAR penalty
legislation.citation: FA 2013 s212A (inserted by FA 2016 s158(2)); value of counteracted advantage in Sch 43C
legislation.what_it_does: Where a tax return was made on the basis of a tax advantage later counteracted under the GAAR (after the Sch 43, 43A or 43B notice procedure), the person is liable to a penalty of 60% of the value of the counteracted advantage.
legislation.relevance: Using an abusive scheme risks the tax, plus interest, plus a 60% penalty; abusive schemes are not a free option.
legislation.status: Law (in force since 15 September 2016).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2004 Part 7: Disclosure of Tax Avoidance Schemes (DOTAS)
legislation.what_it_does: Promoters (or users, where there is no UK promoter) must disclose 'notifiable arrangements' to HMRC (ss308-310): arrangements within prescribed hallmarks where a tax advantage is expected to be one of the main benefits (s306). HMRC allocate a scheme reference number (s311); the promoter must give it to the client within 30 days (s312), and each user must report it to HMRC (s313).
legislation.relevance: A scheme reference number means a disclosed avoidance scheme, not HMRC approval; HMRC's 'Tax avoidance: an introduction' lists it as a warning sign, and DOTAS schemes can trigger an accelerated payment notice (FA 2014 s219). Refuse to recommend any such scheme.
legislation.status: Law (in force; amended by FA 2026 ss216-217 from 18 March 2026).

legislation.name: ITTOIA 2005 ss23A-23H and F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 12: self-employed disguised remuneration and the loan charge
legislation.citation: ITTOIA 2005 ss23A-23H (inserted by F(No.2)A 2017 s35); F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 12 (with Sch 11 for employees, ITEPA Part 7A); amended by FA 2020 ss15-17
legislation.what_it_does: ITTOIA s23A applies where a trader is party to an arrangement connected with the trade that provides relevant benefits (such as loans) through a third party and a tax advantage is a reasonable expectation; s23E then taxes the benefit as trade profits. Sch 12 treats third-party loans to traders made between 9 December 2010 and 5 April 2017 and still outstanding at 5 April 2019 as a relevant benefit arising then (the loan charge). FA 2020 added an election to spread the charge over three years and an exclusion for reasonably disclosed years.
legislation.relevance: Any loan, advance or third-party payment received in return for self-employed work is taxable trade income; trade-based schemes have their own rules and dates. Refuse any such arrangement and, for past use, point to HMRC's settlement routes.
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2026 ss25-27 and SI 2026/821: Loan Charge Settlement Scheme
legislation.citation: FA 2026 (c. 11) ss25-27; Employment and Trading Income etc. (Loan Charge Settlement Scheme) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/821)
legislation.what_it_does: Requires a loan charge settlement scheme, created by SI 2026/821 (in force 5 August 2026). HMRC must offer settlement to anyone it believes is liable to F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 11/12 loan charge amounts, unless it reasonably suspects them of being (or directing) a DOTAS promoter or introducer. Tax and NIC are recalculated for the years the scheme money was attributed to; each year's figure is reduced by 10% of the first £50,000 and 5% of the next £100,000 of scheme amounts attributed to that year, then the total by a further £5,000, with the total reduction capped at £70,000. Accrued interest and most penalties are written off (HMRC may require deliberate-and-concealed penalties to be paid). A first offer is open for 90 days, a further offer 30 days; interest runs on late-paid settlement amounts.
legislation.relevance: If the user used a contractor or umbrella loan scheme in the past, this is the lawful, often much cheaper way out; direct them to it and to independent advice. Using a statutory settlement is not avoidance.
legislation.status: Law (FA 2026 ss25-27 since Royal Assent 18 March 2026; SI 2026/821 made 14 July 2026, in force 5 August 2026).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2026 Part 6 Chs 1-2 (ss159-176): prohibition on promoting certain tax avoidance arrangements; promoter action notices
legislation.citation: FA 2026 ss159-165 (prohibition; civil penalties s162; criminal offence s163); ss166-176 (promoter action notices)
legislation.what_it_does: A person must not promote arrangements marketed as giving a tax advantage where there is no realistic prospect of achieving it, or arrangements of a kind specified in HMRC regulations (s159(1)-(2)); whether the promoter knows this is irrelevant (s159(5)). Breach attracts civil penalties (s162) and is a criminal offence with up to 2 years' imprisonment on indictment (s163). ss166-176 provide promoter action notices.
legislation.relevance: The boundary in its strongest current terms: the assistant and the app must never suggest, market or describe as workable any arrangement with no realistic prospect of success. If the user is approached by a promoter, point them to HMRC's reporting route.
legislation.status: Law (Royal Assent 18 March 2026; s159(1) in force from 18 May 2026 (s165(2)); the remaining provisions from Royal Assent).

legislation.name: Finance (No. 2) Act 2017 Schedule 16: penalties for enablers of defeated tax avoidance
legislation.what_it_does: Once abusive tax arrangements (a GAAR-style double reasonableness test) are defeated, each enabler (designers, managers, marketers, enabling participants, financial enablers) is liable to a penalty equal to the consideration received for enabling them; most categories require that they knew, or could reasonably be expected to know, the arrangements were abusive.
legislation.relevance: Facilitating avoidance is penalised, not just using it; another reason the assistant must not design, recommend or market abusive arrangements to anyone.
legislation.status: Law (arrangements entered into on or after 16 November 2017; not amended by FA 2026).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2014 Part 4: follower notices and accelerated payment notices
legislation.what_it_does: HMRC can issue a follower notice where a final judicial ruling defeats materially similar arrangements (s204); not taking corrective action incurs a penalty of 30% of the denied advantage (ss208-209). HMRC can issue an accelerated payment notice where a follower notice, DOTAS or a GAAR counteraction applies (s219), requiring the disputed tax to be paid up front while the dispute continues.
legislation.relevance: Scheme users lose the cash-flow benefit and pay the tax before the dispute is resolved, a concrete reason avoidance schemes rarely pay off.
legislation.status: Law (in force; s209 amended by FA 2021 Sch 28).

legislation.name: Theft Act 1968 s32(1)(a): preservation of cheating the public revenue
legislation.what_it_does: Abolished the common-law offence of cheating except as regards offences relating to the public revenue, keeping the common-law offence of cheating the public revenue, whose penalty is at large (no statutory maximum).
legislation.relevance: The statutory basis for the most serious tax-evasion charge (see Mavji, Dimsey, Dosanjh). Refuse any request to hide income, falsify records or mislead HMRC.
legislation.status: Law (in force, England and Wales).

legislation.name: Criminal Finances Act 2017 s45: failure to prevent facilitation of UK tax evasion
legislation.what_it_does: A relevant body is guilty of an offence if a person associated with it, acting in that capacity, commits a UK tax evasion facilitation offence, unless it had reasonable prevention procedures. UK tax evasion offences include cheating the public revenue and being knowingly concerned in fraudulent evasion (s45(4)).
legislation.relevance: Production companies, agencies and umbrella companies the freelancer deals with, and any company operating this app, need procedures against facilitating evasion; a further reason to refuse and flag facilitation requests.
legislation.status: Law (in force since 30 September 2017; no outstanding effects).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2026 ss4-7 and 10: income tax rates and thresholds
legislation.what_it_does: s10 freezes the basic rate limit at £37,700 and the personal allowance at £12,570 to 2030-31. s4 raises dividend ordinary and upper rates to 10.75% and 35.75% from 2026-27 (additional rate stays 39.35%). ss5-7 set 2027-28 savings rates, and new property income rates, at 22/42/47%.
legislation.relevance: Trading profits are still taxed at 20/40/45% (England, Wales and Northern Ireland; Scottish rates differ), with the higher rate starting at £50,270 to 2030-31. Dividend and savings rates matter when comparing sole trading with incorporation, and for interest on business savings. Budget 2026 proposes raising the 2027-28 savings and property rates further to 24/44/49% (not law).
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: National Insurance Contributions (Reduction in Rates) Act 2023 s3: Class 2 abolished as a compulsory charge from 6 April 2024
legislation.citation: NIC (Reduction in Rates) Act 2023 (c. 57), s3 (amending SSCBA 1992 s11); Royal Assent 18 December 2023
