legislation.what_it_does: From 6 April 2024 self-employed people no longer have to pay Class 2. If profits are at or above the small profits threshold they are treated as having paid it for benefit purposes; if below, they may pay voluntary Class 2 (SSCBA s11(5A)-(6)).
legislation.relevance: No Class 2 is due from 2024-25, and a qualifying year still accrues if profits are at least the threshold: £6,725 (2024-25), £6,845 (2025-26), £7,105 (2026-27). In a low-profit year, voluntary Class 2 at £3.45/£3.50/£3.65 a week is a very cheap, legal way to protect state pension compared with Class 3 at £17.45/£17.75/£18.40. In 2023-24 Class 2 was still compulsory at £3.45 a week, but only where profits were over £12,570; from £6,725 up to that it was treated as paid (SSCBA s11(2), (5A)-(5B)).
legislation.status: Law (in force from 6 April 2024).

legislation.name: National Insurance Contributions (Reduction in Rates) Act 2024 s1: Class 4 main rate cut to 6% from 6 April 2024
legislation.citation: NIC (Reduction in Rates) Act 2024 (c. 5), s1(3) (amending SSCBA 1992 s15(3ZA)); Royal Assent 20 March 2024
legislation.what_it_does: From 6 April 2024 the main Class 4 rate fell from 9% to 6% (replacing the 8% enacted in 2023), on profits between £12,570 and £50,270, with 2% above £50,270 (SSCBA s15).
legislation.relevance: Class 4 is 9% for 2023-24 and 6% for 2024-25 onwards. Each £1 of allowable expense or allowance saves 26p for a basic-rate trader from 2024-25 (20% tax + 6% NIC), 29p in 2023-24, and 42p at the higher rate (40% + 2%).
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: Social Security (Contributions) (Amendment No. 2) Regulations 2026: voluntary Class 2 for periods abroad removed
legislation.citation: SI 2026/294, amending reg 147 of the Social Security (Contributions) Regulations 2001
legislation.what_it_does: From 2026-27, voluntary Class 2 can no longer be paid for periods abroad, except in narrow cases. New Class 3 applications for periods abroad need 10 years' UK residence or 10 years of contributions, though existing Class 2 payers applying before 6 April 2027 can use a 3-year route.
legislation.relevance: Matters only if the user spends a period living or working abroad (for example long international tours); voluntary Class 2 for UK-based low-profit years is unaffected.
legislation.status: Law (in force 6 April 2026 for tax years beginning after 5 April 2026; announced at Budget 2025).

legislation.name: Finance Act 2025 ss7, 8 and 23: CGT rates, Business Asset Disposal Relief, zero-emission car FYA
legislation.citation: Finance Act 2025 (c. 8), ss7, 8, 23; Royal Assent 20 March 2025
legislation.what_it_does: s7 raises the main CGT rates for individuals to 18% and 24%. s8 raises the BADR rate to 14% for disposals from 6 April 2025 and to 18% from 6 April 2026. s23 extended the 100% FYA for new zero-emission cars to 5 April 2026 for income tax (FA 2026 s30 then extended it to 5 April 2027).
legislation.relevance: Little effect on day-to-day trading; relevant if the business or a chargeable business asset is sold or the trade ceases. Budget 2026 proposes cutting the BADR lifetime limit to £500,000 from 6 April 2027 (proposed, not law).
legislation.status: Law (in force).

legislation.name: Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 s5: High Income Child Benefit Charge thresholds raised to £60,000 and £80,000
legislation.citation: Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 (c. 12), s5 (ITEPA 2003 ss681B-681C); Royal Assent 24 May 2024
legislation.what_it_does: From 2024-25 the charge starts when adjusted net income exceeds £60,000 and recovers all the Child Benefit at £80,000 (1% per £200 over £60,000).
legislation.relevance: Applies only if the user or a partner claims Child Benefit. Pension contributions and Gift Aid reduce adjusted net income and so legitimately reduce the charge.
legislation.status: Law (in force for 2024-25 onwards; current figures in ITEPA ss681B-681C as at the legislation.gov.uk revision of 22 Sep 2026).

guidance.name: HMRC BIM37007: apportionment — identifiable part versus dual purpose
guidance.what_it_says: If a definite part or proportion of an expense is wholly and exclusively for the trade, that part is allowed (ITTOIA s34(2)); expenditure with an inseparable dual purpose is wholly disallowed, with no business proportion. HMRC accepts a statistical approach from a representative period for motor expenses and use of home, used until circumstances change.
guidance.relevance: Split costs where the business element is identifiable (car running costs by business-mileage share, phone or broadband by usage, a hotel bill by business nights) and keep a sample-period record to support the percentages; do not apportion intrinsically dual items such as clothing or ordinary meals.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law), checked 24 Nov 2026. Section text last changed 1 April 2016; 'Updated 4 August 2026' is the manual-wide date.

guidance.name: HMRC BIM37910: clothing — everyday wardrobe versus uniform, costume and protective clothing
guidance.what_it_says: Ordinary clothing that could form part of a hypothetical person's everyday wardrobe is disallowed, even if worn only for work or required by professional rules (Mallalieu); protective clothing and uniforms are allowed. Performer costumes are covered at BIM50160.
guidance.relevance: Black jeans, T-shirts and plain show blacks are disallowed; PPE (safety boots, gloves, hard hats, hi-vis, fall-arrest kit) and branded crew uniforms are allowed.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law), interpreting ITTOIA s34(1)(a) and Mallalieu v Drummond.

guidance.name: HMRC BIM37670, BIM37675 and BIM37677: itinerant traders, sub-contractors, and renting accommodation while away
guidance.what_it_says: Meals away from base are generally disallowed (Caillebotte), but reasonable costs are allowed for itinerant trades and occasional journeys outside the normal pattern (ITTOIA s57A). Where a business trip needs a night away from home, hotel accommodation and reasonable overnight subsistence are deductible, but not accommodation at the base of operations (Mason v Tyson, Prior v Saunders, McLaren v Mumford). A sub-contractor working at two or more sites a year can normally deduct home-to-site travel; if one site is the normal pattern, only if home is in a real sense the base. Lunches on a regular local pattern and subsistence for long-term work in one area away from home are disallowed. BIM37677: rented accommodation is not automatically excluded, but is deductible only where its sole purpose is the trade (Healy).
guidance.relevance: A crew member with many venues a year is in HMRC's 'normally allowed' category. If a year becomes dominated by one site or one client's depot, expect a challenge unless home is clearly the business centre (contracts, prep, kit, admin and other clients run from home). On tours, accommodation and reasonable meals are allowed; keep receipts and job references.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law). Section text last changed: BIM37670 1 April 2016; BIM37675 14 December 2018; BIM37677 16 June 2026. The statutory rule for meals (ITTOIA s57A) is law.

guidance.name: HMRC BIM37600-BIM37635: travel costs, duality and home to work
guidance.what_it_says: Travel between home and a place of work is generally disallowed because it serves the private choice of where to live; working at home or keeping records and tools there does not change this (BIM37605 Newsom; BIM37635 Powell v Jackman). For an itinerant trader moving between temporary, unpredictable sites, HMRC allows travel between home and those sites (BIM37620 Horton v Young), but not where home is outside the area in which the trade is carried on or the places of work are fixed and predictable. Stopping at a supplier does not turn a commute into a business journey (BIM37630). A trip partly for a holiday fails entirely (BIM37610, Bowden v Russell & Russell), though a definite business part of a mixed cost such as a car's business mileage can still be apportioned under s34(2) (BIM37600).
guidance.relevance: For short engagements at varying venues HMRC's own guidance accepts home-to-venue travel by an itinerant trader with a home base; quote BIM37620 in any enquiry. Do not tack a holiday onto a work trip if the fare is to be claimed.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law).

guidance.name: HMRC BIM47700-BIM47705: travel and subsistence — meals and accommodation (including the night before an early call)
guidance.what_it_says: Food, drink and accommodation are normally living costs and cannot be split to claim an 'extra cost' element. Under ITTOIA s57A, reasonable food and drink is deductible only if travel to the place is (or would be) deductible and the trade is itinerant or the trip is occasional and outside the normal pattern. Separately, as HMRC practice based on case law (BIM37670: Edwards v Warmsley, Henshall & Co (1967) 44 TC 431; Watkis v Ashford, Sparkes & Harward (1985) 58 TC 468), where a business trip necessitates nights away from home, hotel accommodation and reasonable overnight subsistence (including meals taken with the stay) are deductible, but not accommodation at the base of trade operations. BIM47705 does not specifically mention the night before an early call.
guidance.relevance: A night before an early call is covered only if the job actually makes the stay necessary: the venue is a temporary place of work (so travel there is deductible), the stay is for the job not personal reasons (Healy 2015; Taylor [18]), and the hotel is not at a base of operations. Keep the call sheet or PO with call time and venue, distance and travel time, the hotel invoice and meal receipts, and note why commuting was not practicable. A hotel near a local, commutable venue is open to challenge.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law). BIM47705 section last changed 27 November 2018. s57A is law (SI 2009/730); the overnight accommodation rule is HMRC practice based on case law.

guidance.name: HMRC BIM35901 and BIM35415: capital/revenue summary tests, including short-life assets
guidance.what_it_says: There is no single test: HMRC looks at what was obtained (an identifiable asset), whether spending acquires, improves or disposes of an asset, whether the benefit endures in the way fixed capital does, and recurrence. A tangible asset with an economic life of under one year should be accepted as revenue (BIM35415, citing Hinton v Maden & Ireland (1959) 38 TC 391).
guidance.relevance: Consumables and short-life items (gaffer tape, batteries, lamps, gels, cable ties, cheap tools that wear out within a year) are revenue on any basis. Durable kit is capital on the accruals basis but deductible on the cash basis under s33A.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law; binds neither taxpayers nor tribunals). Substantive text unchanged since 1 April 2016.

guidance.name: HMRC BIM35660: proprietor's training courses
guidance.what_it_says: Training that updates existing expertise, or provides new expertise within the owner's existing business area (including keeping pace with technology), is revenue; ancillary courses such as bookkeeping or digital skills may be too. Training for a new, unrelated business area is unlikely to be allowable (Dass).
guidance.relevance: Certification renewals, new console or software training, and health-and-safety courses for event work are deductible; a course to retrain into an unrelated career is not.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law); section last updated 6 March 2024 when worked examples were added.

guidance.name: HMRC BIM72005-BIM72050: cash basis from 2024-25 (overview, capital expenditure, rules not applied)
guidance.what_it_says: The cash basis is the default from 6 April 2024. Receipts and expenses can be dated consistently by payment date or bank-statement date; mixed costs must be apportioned; VAT can be treated net or gross, consistently. Capital expenditure is allowable except for the s33A exclusions; cars stay in capital allowances provided the mileage rate has not been claimed. The car-hire restriction does not apply.
guidance.relevance: Confirms how the app should treat transaction dates, VAT, equipment and cars for 2024-25 onwards. Guidance for 2023-24 and earlier is at BIM70005-BIM70100.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance matching the legislation in force (checked 23-24 Nov 2026).

guidance.name: HMRC BIM75005: simplified expenses for motor vehicles (rates for 2026-27 and earlier)
guidance.what_it_says: The mileage rate covers buying, running, insurance, road tax, MOT, repairs and depreciation, and is optional on either basis. Once used it must continue for that vehicle until the vehicle is replaced; it is barred if capital allowances were ever claimed on the vehicle. Tolls, congestion charges and parking are allowed on top. Rates: 55p and 25p (motorcycles 24p) for 2026-27; 45p and 25p up to 2025-26, with worked examples for non-tax-year accounting periods.
guidance.relevance: The app should lock the method per vehicle, require a contemporaneous business-mileage log, add parking and tolls separately, and compare the mileage rate with actual costs plus capital allowances before the first claim for a new vehicle.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance matching enacted legislation (55p is law under TEVA 2026 s2).

guidance.name: HMRC BIM75010 and BIM47820: use of home — flat rate or actual costs
guidance.what_it_says: A sole trader working from home 25 or more hours a month can choose the flat rate (£10 for 25-50 hours, £18 for 51-100, £26 for 101 or more, counting only hours wholly and exclusively on qualifying work such as providing services, keeping records and marketing) instead of actual household running costs. Fixed costs (council tax, insurance, mortgage interest but not capital, rent, general repairs) and the business share of phone and broadband can still be claimed where a business proportion is identifiable. Under actual costs (BIM47820), fixed costs are allowable only where part of the home is set aside solely for the trade for a specific period, normally apportioned by area and time; running costs (cleaning, heat, light, power, metered water) are apportioned on the facts, with any reasonable estimate accepted for minor use and a higher share where power-hungry equipment is used. Telephone and broadband are not household costs: business calls and a business share of line rental and internet are allowable, or the full cost where private use is not significant.
guidance.relevance: Supports a best-of-both approach: flat rate (or actual running costs) plus the business share of fixed costs and broadband. Before recommending exclusive business use of a room, flag the possible effect on CGT private residence relief on a sale. BIM47820 (and BIM70040) still mention the £500 cash-basis interest cap, which applies only to 2023-24 (abolished from 2024-25 by FA 2024 Sch 10 para 7).
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law). BIM47820 content last updated 1 May 2025. The flat rate rests on ITTOIA s94H.

guidance.name: GOV.UK: Cash basis — who can use it and how to opt for traditional accounting
guidance.what_it_says: Cash basis is the standard method for sole traders and partnerships without corporate partners. Excluded businesses include limited companies, LLPs, those with herd-basis or averaging elections, BPRA within 7 years, mineral extraction and R&D allowances. A trader opting for traditional accounting says so on the Self Assessment return; adjustments may arise on switching.
guidance.relevance: The plain-English source to show the user; supports a legitimate yearly method-choice review, with switching adjustments.
guidance.status: Current GOV.UK guidance accurately reflecting FA 2024 Sch 10 (2024-25 onwards); no 'last updated' date shown.

guidance.name: HMRC BIM81310 and BIM81320: transition profits — excluded from net income, taxed by notional calculation
guidance.what_it_says: Spread transition profits are left out of 'net income' to reduce the impact on benefits and allowances. The tax on them is the difference between a calculation without them and a notional calculation with them; that notional calculation can reduce the personal allowance where income is over £100,000, so the extra tax can exceed the basic rate (HMRC Example 24). Overlap relief can only be used in 2023-24. BIM81310 gives the formula for reducing later years after an acceleration election.
guidance.relevance: When modelling bringing forward transition profit, use the two-calculation method rather than simply adding the profit to income. The researcher infers (not explicit in BIM81320) that keeping the amounts out of net income also keeps them out of adjusted net income for HICBC.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (GOV.UK 'Work out your transition profit' updated 5 November 2024), backed by FA 2022 Sch 1 para 75, for 2023-24 to 2027-28.

guidance.name: HMRC BIM85705: trade losses — the 'commercial basis' test
guidance.what_it_says: HMRC treats ITA s66 as aimed at activities that lack commercial inspiration. Following Wannell v Rothwell, 'commercial' means not uncommercial (not 'profitable'), tested by how a business of that type would normally be run; HMRC also looks for non-commercial motives such as a hobby interest.
guidance.relevance: Shows the evidence HMRC will ask for if a loss claim is enquired into; use it as a checklist before recommending sideways relief.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law). Section unchanged since 3 October 2018; partly out of date: it still says 'throughout the basis period', changed to 'throughout the tax year' from 2024-25 by FA 2022 Sch 1 para 42, and cites no case after Wannell.

guidance.name: HMRC ESM4120: behind-camera roles normally treated as self-employed (Appendix 1 'Lists of Roles')
guidance.what_it_says: HMRC treats a listed film or TV behind-camera role as self-employed if the role's Column A criterion or the Column B conditions (ESM4115) are met. Column A for crew roles: substantial equipment without extra fee (camera crew, DIT/data, Steadicam, drone); substantial equipment or the Hall v Lorimer conditions (vision mixer, vision engineer, sound roles); substantial equipment (electrician, gaffer, lighting hand, grips, riggers, EVS, video technician, satellite operator); multiple or overlapping clients and no client right to switch tasks (console, lighting desk, rigging desk and dimmer operators, floor manager, playback/DAW operators); providing facilities (OB manager). Safety divers: self-employed for income tax but usually Class 1 NIC.
guidance.relevance: The first check for bookings with TV and film production companies; under Column B any listed role on a specific production for a finite period also qualifies. The list is guidance, not exhaustive, and does not cover live events, corporate events or concerts, which are judged on general principles (ESM0500). HMRC says it will stand by a CEST result if the information entered is accurate.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law). First published 19 June 2026, last updated 7 October 2026; replaces the withdrawn ESM4118.

guidance.name: HMRC ESM4115: behind-camera roles — specific production, finite period, discrete engagement
guidance.what_it_says: For roles marked 'Refer to ESM4115' in Column B, HMRC accepts self-employment where the engagement is on a specific production (a feature film, single drama or documentary, commercial, music video, or a single programme or series at a specific interval for a fixed term) for a finite period tied to a deliverable or project completion rather than a set number of days. Re-engagements must be discrete, not part of an overarching longer-term agreement; a gap, dependence on outside factors such as finance, or a retender point to separate engagements, but none is decisive. Rostering by short-notice offers is not an overarching agreement if each assignment is separate.
guidance.relevance: Central to longer engagements with one client: each job should be a genuinely separate booking for a named production with an end set by the deliverable. Rolling month-by-month or open-ended arrangements, or an umbrella agreement with a production company, put self-employed treatment at risk. Engagements with different group companies count separately unless for the same production.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law); last updated 7 October 2026.

guidance.name: HMRC ESM4116: behind-camera short-term engagements and NI-only deductions
guidance.what_it_says: Crew outside the list (for example not providing their own equipment) who work a succession of short engagements of 10 days or less for many clients, consistent with Lorimer, can be treated as self-employed and can ask HMRC to confirm this. Where an engager has decided a booking is employment, HMRC allows NI-only deductions (NIC but no tax) if the engagement lasts 7 days or less (counting rest days in between) with no pre-arranged pattern of regular engagement.
guidance.relevance: A route to self-employed treatment for a technician without own kit. If a production makes NI-only deductions on a short booking it has treated that booking as employment: flag it, keep it out of trading turnover, and help report it correctly.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law); last updated 7 October 2026.

guidance.name: HMRC ESM4117: Appendix 1 definitions — substantial equipment, tools of the trade, premises
guidance.what_it_says: For Appendix 1 roles, 'substantial provision of materials/equipment' means major items of significant value that play a fundamental role in the grade's work and are an integral requirement of the contract; tools of the trade are excluded, even if valuable. The kit should generally be owned by the worker or permanently at their disposal; hired kit counts only if obtained entirely independently of the engager, and is disregarded if the engager effectively underwrites the risk (an increased rate, a box payment or a hire agreement). It applies only to the Appendix 1 list, not as a general legal test.
guidance.relevance: If a PO pays a separate kit-hire or box-rental line, HMRC disregards that kit for status; owning substantial kit and supplying it within an all-in rate supports self-employment. Check how the PO describes kit and keep an asset register (which also supports capital allowances).
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law); section unchanged since 20 December 2019.

guidance.name: HMRC ESM4104 and ESM4110: service companies in film and TV; HMRC's Film and Production Unit
guidance.what_it_says: ESM4104 tells HMRC staff that many film and video workers in 'employed' grades set up limited companies to avoid PAYE and Class 1 NIC, that these arrangements often fail with the worker remaining an employee of the production company, and that otherwise officers should consider the intermediaries (IR35) rules in ITEPA Part 2 Ch 8. ESM4110 gives the status-enquiry contact: Film and Production Unit, SO733, Newcastle NE98 1ZZ; a.filmproductionunitmailbox@hmrc.gov.uk; 0300 123 2326 (option 1).
guidance.relevance: Setting up a company does not get anyone out of employment status; never suggest it as a status workaround. The unit is the official route for the user to have HMRC confirm their status.
guidance.status: Current HMRC internal guidance (not law); text unchanged since 2020 and pre-dates the April 2021 private-sector off-payroll rules.

guidance.name: HMRC ESM0551: personal factors and the effect of Lorimer on short-term engagements
guidance.what_it_says: Lorimer is particularly relevant where the worker provides similar services to many engagers, both sides intend self-employment, and the worker runs a business-like operation with costs not normally associated with employment. Supporting pointers: many short engagements, rare skill, engagement for a specific task, heavy travel costs to varied workplaces, risk of late payment or bad debt, and ability to influence rates.
guidance.relevance: An evidence checklist the app can track from its own data: number of distinct clients and POs a year, booking lengths, invoices paid late or unpaid, travel to varied venues, and evidence of rate negotiation.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law); unchanged since January 2016.

guidance.name: HMRC ESM0553: regularly working for one engager
guidance.what_it_says: A run of short contracts that are each self-employed can be replaced by an overarching contract of employment if the person starts working virtually full-time for one engager; but someone building a business who can, for now, only get work from one engager is not necessarily employed.
guidance.relevance: The main risk in the user's long engagements with one client: monitor each client's share of income and days and warn when one production company dominates for a long period.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law); section last updated 14 April 2021.

guidance.name: HMRC ESM10006 and ESM10006A: medium or large clients under the off-payroll rules (thresholds from 6 April 2025)
guidance.what_it_says: Small non-public-sector clients do not apply the Chapter 10 rules. For financial years beginning on or after 6 April 2025 a company is medium or large if it exceeds two of: £15m turnover, £7.5m balance sheet total, 50 employees (previously £10.2m and £5.1m) for two consecutive years, judged from the last financial year whose filing deadline fell before the tax year began.
guidance.relevance: Only relevant if the user ever works through their own company: it decides whether the production company issues a status determination (medium or large) or the user's company applies IR35 itself under Chapter 8 (small).
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance, last updated 21 April 2026. The thresholds are law (Companies Act 2006 s382(3) as amended by SI 2024/1303, applied by ITEPA s60A).

guidance.name: GOV.UK: Penalties for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
guidance.what_it_says: Each missed quarterly update or return deadline earns one point; at 4 points (quarterly) there is a £200 penalty, and £200 for each further miss; non-MTD annual filers will have a 2-point threshold. No points for late quarterly updates in the first MTD year, but a late return still earns one. Points below the threshold expire after 24 months; at the threshold, all reset after 12 months of compliance plus catching up any outstanding submissions. Late payment penalties do not apply to payments on account. First MTD year: 30 days before any late payment penalty, then 15 days. 2026-27 rates: 3% of tax unpaid at day 15, a further 3% at day 30, then 10% a year from day 31; 2027-28: 4% and 4% plus 10% a year. A time-to-pay plan pauses penalties. From April 2027 the new penalties apply to everyone who submits a personal SA return.
guidance.relevance: The practical rulebook from 2026-27 or 2027-28. The assistant's penalty estimator should track points, quarterly deadlines (7 Aug, 7 Nov, 7 Feb, 7 May) and payment windows, and use the regime for the correct year.
guidance.status: Guidance current (last updated 19 Nov 2026). LAW for people mandated into MTD in 2026-27 (SI 2026/370 commences FA 2021 Schs 24-27 from 1 April 2026; 3%/3%/10% rates under SI 2025/589). ANNOUNCED ONLY, with no regulations found on legislation.gov.uk: the 4%/4% rates for 2027-28; the regime for those first mandated from 6 April 2027; and the regime for non-MTD SA filers from April 2027. First-year concessions appear in guidance, not statute.

guidance.name: GOV.UK: Check if you're eligible for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
guidance.what_it_says: MTD for Income Tax applies to those with qualifying income over £50,000 in 2024-25 from 6 April 2026, over £30,000 in 2025-26 from 6 April 2027, and over £20,000 in 2026-27 from 6 April 2028.
guidance.relevance: Decides which penalty regime and record-keeping duty applies to the freelancer in each year.
guidance.status: Current guidance (last updated 26 March 2026); thresholds are in law (SI 2026/336).

guidance.name: GOV.UK: HMRC interest rates for late and early payments
guidance.what_it_says: Late payment interest has been Bank of England base rate plus 4% since 6 April 2025 (previously plus 2.5%). Bank Rate rose from 3.75% to 4.00% on 5 November 2026, so for income tax late payment interest is 8.00% from 24 November 2026 (7.75% from 9 January 2026) and repayment interest is 3.00%.
guidance.relevance: Interest runs on late balancing payments and payments on account even where no penalty applies; use date-ranged rates when estimating it. Paying on time, or reducing payments on account where profits genuinely fall, is a legal way to save money.
guidance.status: Current published rates (page updated 6 November 2026); the formula is law (SI 2025/386).

guidance.name: HMRC Compliance Handbook CH160950: reasonable excuse case law
guidance.what_it_says: HMRC adopt the Perrin four-stage test: HMRC must first prove the penalty event, then the taxpayer must show facts that objectively amount to a reasonable excuse for that taxpayer. Following Marlow Rowing Club v HMRC [2020] UKUT 20 (TCC), each case turns on its facts. (The page mistypes Perrin as '[2018] UKUT 156 [TC]'.)
guidance.relevance: Citing HMRC's own guidance in a penalty appeal letter strengthens the case at the HMRC review stage.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law); section text last changed 29 September 2021 (the 23 Nov 2026 header date is the handbook-wide date).

guidance.name: GOV.UK: Business records if you're self-employed — how long to keep your records
guidance.what_it_says: Keep records at least 5 years after the 31 January deadline for the tax year; if the return is sent more than 4 years after the deadline, keep them for 15 months after sending it. If records are lost, give best estimates and tell HMRC they are estimated or provisional.
guidance.relevance: Sets retention rules for the app's document store: for example, 2023-24 records are kept until at least 31 January 2030.
guidance.status: Current guidance; legal basis TMA 1970 s12B.

guidance.name: HMRC Self Assessment Legal Framework manual SALF920: MTD for Income Tax legislation
guidance.what_it_says: The Income Tax (Digital Requirements) Regulations 2021 (SI 2021/1076, amended by SI 2024/167) were revoked and replaced by the Income Tax (Digital Obligations) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/336) from 1 April 2026; SI 2026/356 appointed 1 April 2026 for the relevant F(No.2)A 2017 provisions.
guidance.relevance: Cite SI 2026/336, not the 2021 regulations, for current MTD digital record and quarterly update duties.
guidance.status: Current guidance (last updated 13 October 2026) reflecting SIs in force.

guidance.name: HMRC VAT Notice 733: Flat Rate Scheme, and sector percentages relevant to an events/production technician
guidance.what_it_says: The trader picks the sector that most closely describes the coming year's business, and HMRC will not change a reasonable choice retrospectively (ss4.1-4.2). First-year registrants deduct 1% (s4.7). Capital goods costing £2,000 or more including VAT can have their VAT reclaimed outside the scheme (s15.2). Possible sectors: 'Any other activity not listed elsewhere' 12%, 'Business services not listed elsewhere' 12%, 'Entertainment or journalism' 12.5%, 'Film, radio, television or video production' 13%, 'Photography' 11%, 'Hiring or renting goods' 9.5%; limited cost business rate 16.5%.
guidance.relevance: If the FRS is used, record the reasoning for the sector choice (JJK Engineering). In practice the 16.5% limited-cost rate will often apply; a single kit purchase of £2,000 or more can still have its VAT reclaimed.
guidance.status: Current guidance (last updated 18 December 2025); the sector percentages have legal force under VAT Regulations 1995 reg 55K.

guidance.name: HM Treasury and HMRC, 'Tackling tax avoidance, evasion, and other forms of non-compliance' (March 2019), with HMRC 'Tax avoidance: an introduction'
guidance.what_it_says: Para 1.13: tax evasion is always illegal (deliberately not declaring or accounting for what is owed); tax avoidance is bending the rules of the tax system to gain a tax advantage Parliament never intended, often through contrived, artificial transactions; tax planning is using tax reliefs for the purpose for which they were intended (for example relief on capital investment, ISAs and pension contributions). HMRC's introduction lists warning signs: too good to be true; pay as loans or other untaxed payments; artificial or circular arrangements; misleading claims; a scheme reference number; non-compliant umbrella companies.
guidance.relevance: The official three-way classification the assistant should apply and explain to the user.
guidance.status: Current official guidance (not law). Policy paper of 13 March 2019 presented under FA 2019 ss92-93; HMRC introduction last updated 26 May 2022.

guidance.name: HMRC General Anti-Abuse Rule guidance (Parts A-C, approved by the GAAR Advisory Panel)
guidance.what_it_says: Taxpayers frequently have a choice of how to carry out transactions with different tax results, and the GAAR does not challenge such choices unless abusive (B11.1). Where legislation reflects a clear policy of giving relief for certain actions, such as investing in plant and machinery or a pension, reasonable steps to obtain that relief are a reasonable course of action (C5.6.2). The view that exploiting drafting defects is acceptable because it is for HMRC and the drafter to get the legislation right is not reasonable (C5.10.5). Contrived steps taken only to avoid an unfair 'bear trap' charge are generally not abusive (B12.2).
guidance.relevance: Courts must take this guidance into account (FA 2013 s211). It gives authoritative wording for both sides: choosing between statutory options and claiming reliefs as designed is fine; exploiting loopholes is not.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law). Parts A-C and E effective from 16 July 2021; Part D from 11 September 2020.

guidance.name: GAAR Advisory Panel opinion of 11 October 2018: contractor rewards using loans (Mr N), and HMRC Spotlight 46
guidance.what_it_says: A contractor was 'employed' by a trust company on minimum wage, with about £83,000 of a £110,000 fee paid as 'loans' whose creditor rights were assigned to an EFRBS, giving a marketed take-home of 79-82%. The Panel found the steps contrived and abnormal, aimed at a perceived shortcoming in ITEPA Part 7A, and both entering into and carrying out the arrangements were not a reasonable course of action. Spotlight 46 (16 January 2019) says such schemes do not work.
guidance.relevance: The contractor pattern the assistant should recognise and refuse: a small taxed wage plus a large 'loan', a promised 75-85% take-home, offshore or trust routing, and a high margin.
guidance.status: Published GAAR Advisory Panel opinion (advisory, not binding precedent); the gap was later closed by statute and such loans are subject to the 2019 loan charge.

guidance.name: GAAR Advisory Panel opinion of 29 July 2026: disguised remuneration arrangements using dual payments (enablers of defeated tax avoidance)
guidance.what_it_says: The Panel's opinion is that entering into and carrying out disguised remuneration arrangements using 'dual payments' (a taxed element plus an untaxed one) is not a reasonable course of action in relation to the relevant tax provisions; given for the enablers-penalty regime (F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 16) in respect of Companies A, B and C. Published 25 August 2026.
guidance.relevance: Shows that in 2026 HMRC is still pursuing disguised remuneration paid as two separate payments and now targets enablers too; matches Spotlight 60's warning about pay arriving as two payments.
guidance.status: Published statutory advisory opinion (not law; binds no tribunal). The latest GAAR Panel opinion on GOV.UK; not superseded.

guidance.name: HMRC 'Tax avoidance schemes currently in the spotlight' (collection), with the Spotlights relevant to contractors and freelancers
guidance.what_it_says: Spotlights describe arrangements HMRC believes do not work and will challenge; users could pay the extra tax, NIC and interest, with penalties for careless or deliberate behaviour, the GAAR 60% penalty in some cases, and follower notices, APNs or litigation. Relevant Spotlights: 42 contractor loan scheme advertising (Feb 2018); 45 umbrella companies offering higher take-home pay (Aug 2018); 46 contrived loan arrangements (Jan 2019); 48 contractor loan settlements and deeds of release (Feb 2019); 49 schemes claiming to avoid the loan charge (Mar 2019); 50 asset transfers to avoid the loan charge (Mar 2019); 55 umbrella comparison and broker websites (Apr 2020); 57 selling future business revenues to a revenue service trust, naming self-employed users (Dec 2020); 60 agency workers and contractors with umbrella companies (Aug 2022); 64 employment agencies using umbrella companies (Apr 2024); 66 LLP arrangements disguising employment income (Oct 2024); 67 managed service companies (Nov 2024); 71 workers moved between umbrella companies (Jun 2025).
guidance.relevance: The assistant's checklist: if a user describes an arrangement matching a Spotlight (loans or annuities for pay, 'enhanced' umbrella options, LLP membership to disguise pay, deeds of release for loan charge debts), name the Spotlight, refuse to help with the scheme, and give HMRC's exit route.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law). Live collection; latest entry 22 April 2026; no Spotlight above 71 found as of 24 Nov 2026.

guidance.name: HMRC Spotlight 60: warning for agency workers and contractors employed by umbrella companies
guidance.what_it_says: Some umbrella companies pay part of a worker's earnings as a 'loan', advance, annuity, grant or other supposedly non-taxable payment, often via offshore third parties. All payments for the work are employment income liable to income tax and NIC; HMRC never approves avoidance schemes and can pursue the worker. Warning signs: short or missing contracts, extra agreements, 'enhanced' options, offers of a percentage take-home such as 80%, more money in the bank than on the payslip, pay arriving as two payments, offshore umbrellas, margins of 15-22%. HMRC advises moving to a compliant umbrella, getting advice (TaxAid for low incomes) and contacting CAGetHelpOutOfTaxAvoidance@hmrc.gov.uk.
guidance.relevance: Gives concrete warning signs for the assistant to check if the user is ever paid through an umbrella.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law); live, not updated since 25 August 2022.

guidance.name: HMRC Spotlight 71: warning for agency workers and contractors moved between umbrella companies
guidance.what_it_says: Non-compliant umbrella companies move workers between entities to hide avoidance. Signs: a sudden change of employer name or PAYE reference; being paid by a different company from the one on the contract; extra agreements such as annuity agreements; payslips showing less pay than the bank account. The worker remains responsible for knowing what tax they should pay.
guidance.relevance: The current HMRC warning for anyone working through umbrellas. The app can compare bank receipts against payslips or PAYE data and flag mismatches without accusing anyone, then suggest contacting HMRC or an independent adviser.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law); Spotlight 71, 13 June 2025; no update or withdrawal shown.

guidance.name: HMRC loan charge guidance 2026: 'The loan charge', the settlement scheme, and how HMRC will implement it
guidance.what_it_says: The loan charge applies to disguised remuneration loans made on or after 9 December 2010, received before 6 April 2017 if self-employed (6 April 2019 if employed), from a third party, not repaid by 5 April 2019 and not settled by 30 September 2020. The 2026 settlement scheme recalculates the tax and gives reductions capped at £70,000 (including a £5,000 reduction); late payment interest, most penalties and some IHT charges are dropped; accepted offers become binding contracts; instalments over up to 5 years are possible.
guidance.relevance: If the user used a contractor loan scheme in the past, explain these official options, encourage contact with HMRC (0300 322 9494; CAGetHelpOutOfTaxAvoidance@hmrc.gov.uk) or an independent adviser, and never suggest schemes claiming to avoid the loan charge (Spotlights 49 and 50).
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (settlement guidance updated 5 November 2026) for a statutory scheme in FA 2026 ss25-27 and SI 2026/821.

guidance.name: HMRC: Named tax avoidance schemes, promoters, enablers and suppliers
guidance.what_it_says: HMRC publishes the names of schemes, promoters, enablers and suppliers, schemes subject to stop notices, and example marketing material. It is not a complete list, absence from it does not mean a scheme works, and HMRC does not approve tax avoidance schemes for use.
guidance.relevance: When a user names an umbrella company, payroll provider or 'tax-efficient' offer, suggest checking this list, but never treat absence from it as clearance.
guidance.status: Current guidance (not law), updated 19 November 2026; power to publish in FA 2022 s86.

guidance.name: HMRC criminal investigation policy
guidance.what_it_says: HMRC uses civil fraud procedures (Code of Practice 9) where appropriate and reserves criminal investigation for cases needing a strong deterrent, such as deliberate concealment or deception, false or forged documents, avoidance schemes relying on false documents, materially false statements during a civil investigation, and repeat offending. A complete unprompted disclosure favours the civil route; prosecution decisions are made by the CPS, COPFS or PPSNI.
guidance.relevance: Lets the assistant explain plainly that falsifying receipts, mileage logs or invoices moves a matter towards criminal investigation, and that voluntarily correcting past errors is the safer, lawful path.
guidance.status: Current HMRC guidance (not law); last updated 13 July 2021.

developments.name: Mileage rate raised to 55p for the first 10,000 business miles from 2026-27
developments.what_changes: The rate for the first 10,000 business miles in a car or van, for employee AMAPs and self-employed simplified mileage, rises from 45p to 55p, retrospectively from 6 April 2026 (HMRC policy paper 'Increase to Approved Mileage Allowance Payments (AMAPs) and self employed simplified mileage rates', 17 June 2026; enacted by Taxation (Energy and Vehicles) Act 2026 s2, Royal Assent 15 July 2026). The rate above 10,000 miles stays 25p for 2026-27. Budget 2026 confirmed the 55p rate is permanent.
developments.status_note: Law. Use 55p for all 2026-27 business miles, including any logged before the June 2026 announcement; 2023-24 to 2025-26 stay at 45p.

developments.name: Mileage rate above 10,000 business miles to rise from 25p to 35p (Budget 2026)
developments.what_changes: Budget 2026 OOTLAR para 2.7: the simplified mileage rate above 10,000 business miles rises from 25p to 35p from 6 April 2027, to be made by statutory instrument (listed among measures not in Finance Bill 2026-27), with the same change to the NIC disregard for relevant motoring expenditure. Example for 2027-28: 15,000 business miles would give £7,250 (10,000 x 55p + 5,000 x 35p) instead of £6,750 at 25p.
developments.status_note: Announced, not law. Do not apply before 6 April 2027 or until the SI is made; recheck legislation.gov.uk. For 2026-27 the rates are 55p then 25p.

developments.name: Trading allowance to rise from £1,000 to £3,000 from 6 April 2027
developments.what_changes: HMRC policy paper 'Increasing the trading allowance' (28 October 2026) and OOTLAR para 1.5: the trading allowance in ITTOIA s783AD, and the Self Assessment trading reporting threshold, rise from £1,000 to £3,000 from 2027-28, via Finance Bill 2026-27 (Bill 173, introduced 4 November 2026; Committee of the whole House sittings listed for 30 November and 1 December 2026).
developments.status_note: Proposed in a Bill before Parliament, not law. Current law is £1,000 for 2023-24 to 2026-27. Spring 2025 only promised the SA reporting threshold would reach £3,000 by the end of the Parliament; the rise in the allowance itself was announced at Budget 2026.

developments.name: Main-rate FYA to rise to 50% and main-pool WDA to fall to 12% (Budget 2026)
developments.what_changes: HMRC policy paper (29 October 2026) and OOTLAR para 1.42: the main-rate FYA rises from 40% to 50% for expenditure on or after 1 January 2027, and the main-pool WDA falls from 14% to 12% for income tax chargeable periods beginning on or after 6 April 2027, with a hybrid rate for straddling periods; the special rate stays 6%. Via Finance Bill 2026-27 (CAA 2001 ss52(3), 56(1)).
developments.status_note: Proposed, not law, until Finance Bill 2026-27 receives Royal Assent. For 2026-27 the law is 40% FYA and 14% WDA (FA 2026 ss28-29). Mostly irrelevant on the cash basis except for cars, which are excluded from the FYA.

developments.name: Budget 2026: savings and property income rates to rise to 24/44/49% from 2027-28
developments.what_changes: Budget 2026 (HC 726, paras 6.246-6.247) proposes a further 2-point rise in savings income rates to 24/44/49% from 6 April 2027 (UK-wide), and property income rates to 24/44/49% in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, via Finance Bill 2026-27. FA 2026 ss5-7 already set 2027-28 rates at 22/42/47%. Headline income tax, NIC and VAT rates are unchanged.
developments.status_note: Proposed, not law. Affects interest on business savings and any rental income, not trading profits.

developments.name: Budget 2026: 'More Timely Payments' for Self Assessment taxpayers from April 2029
developments.what_changes: OOTLAR para 2.31: more frequent in-year payments for SA taxpayers who make payments on account, from April 2029, replacing the current two payments on account (31 January and 31 July) for those affected.
developments.applies_from: April 2029 (announced; details and legislation to follow)
developments.status_note: Announced only; no legislation yet. Cash-flow planning item, not a tax change.

developments.name: Budget 2026: no late-submission points for first four quarterly updates for April 2027 MTD joiners
developments.what_changes: OOTLAR para 2.36 and Budget 2026 para 6.152: those joining MTD for Income Tax in April 2027 will get no late-submission penalty points for their first four quarterly updates in 2027-28. (HMRC guidance gives a similar first-year concession for 2026-27 joiners.)
developments.status_note: Announced only. A late annual return still earns a point.

developments.name: New points-based penalty regime to apply to all personal Self Assessment returns from 2027-28
developments.what_changes: HMRC guidance (19 November 2026) says that from April 2027 the FA 2021 Sch 24 points-based late submission penalties and Sch 26 late payment penalties will apply to everyone who submits a personal SA return. Under Sch 24 para 5(9) the threshold is 2 points for annual returns and 4 for quarterly ones, with a £200 penalty at the threshold; a person leaving MTD in 2027-28 drops from 4 to 2 points with existing points scaled down (paras 9-13). HMRC guidance also gives late payment rates of 4% at day 15 and 4% at day 30 plus 10% a year from 2027-28 (Autumn Budget 2025 announcement).
developments.status_note: Partly law, partly announced. Law today only for 2026-27 MTD digitally obligated persons (SI 2026/370, from 1 April 2026) and volunteers since 6 April 2024 (SI 2024/440). Extension to non-MTD filers and April 2027 joiners, and the 4%/4% rates, need regulations not yet found on legislation.gov.uk. Sch 55/56 continue to govern 2023-24 to 2025-26 returns, and 2026-27 if not MTD-mandated.

developments.name: Autumn Budget 2025 (26 November 2025): measures and what has since become law
developments.what_changes: Extended the freeze on the personal allowance (£12,570) and basic rate limit (£37,700) to 2030-31; raised dividend ordinary and upper rates by 2 points from 2026-27 (10.75%, 35.75%); set 2027-28 savings and new property income rates at 22/42/47%; cut the main pool WDA from 18% to 14% from 6 April 2026 (income tax, hybrid for straddling periods); added a 40% FYA for new, unused main-rate plant from 1 January 2026 (cars excluded); extended the 100% zero-emission car and charge-point FYA to 5 April 2027 (income tax); removed voluntary Class 2 for periods abroad from 6 April 2026. Penalty reform applies from 2026-27 to MTD-mandated ITSA taxpayers (no late-submission penalties for quarterly updates in 2026-27); extension to all other SA taxpayers from 6 April 2027 and 4% day-15/day-30 late payment penalties from April 2027 were announced.
developments.status_note: Mostly law via Finance Act 2026 and SIs (2026/294, 2026/336, 2026/370). Still only announced: penalty reform for non-MTD SA taxpayers and the 4% late payment rates. The salary-sacrifice NIC cap is in primary legislation with regulations pending.

developments.name: Employment status and media IR35 case law 2023-2026: where things stand in November 2026
developments.what_changes: After PGMOL [2024] UKSC 29, a single short engagement can meet the mutuality and control requirements, and most cases turn on a stage 3 multi-factor weighing of the engagement in the context known to both parties; being in business on own account is relevant but not decisive (S & L Barnes, PD & MJ). HMRC has won on long first-call or exclusive pundit contracts (McCann Media [2024] UKUT 94 (TCC), Barnes, Thompson) and on a short hospital locum engagement (George Mantides [2025] UKUT 124 (TCC)); taxpayers have won where the worker could decline or withdraw without sanction and control was regulatory (PGMOL FTT [2026] UKFTT 654 (TC)), and in a finely balanced case driven by an established independent business (Atholl House [2024] UKFTT 37 (TC)). For a PO-paid technician contracted directly as a sole trader, IR35 and off-payroll do not apply; the only question is whether each engagement is employment. Short, separately booked jobs for many companies, own substantial kit, invoicing risk and no retainer point to self-employment (Hall v Lorimer; ESM4115, ESM4116, ESM4120); long, exclusive, rolling or first-call engagements with one company carry the most risk. Status cannot be chosen to save tax; if an engager gets PAYE wrong, HMRC recovers from the engager under PAYE regulation 80.
developments.status_note: None of the cited decisions has been overruled. Basic Broadcasting is back at the FTT with no remitted decision found; a Bryan Robson UT appeal on image-rights grounds is pending (permission granted December 2025). Later status-related appellate decisions exist (Groom [2026] EWCA Civ 6; Mainpay [2025] EWCA Civ 1290; BlueCrest [2026] UKSC 18) but none is an IR35 decision. The URL is McCann Media [2024] UKUT 94 (TCC).

allowed: Claiming every expense incurred wholly and exclusively for the trade, and the identifiable business share of mixed costs such as car running costs, phone, broadband and hotel bills (ittoia-ss5-34, bim37007).

Choosing between methods Parliament offers: cash basis or accruals (ittoia-ss25b-25c); fixed mileage or actual car costs plus capital allowances (ittoia-ss94d-94g); use-of-home flat rate or actual costs (ittoia-s94h); trading allowance or actual expenses (ittoia-trading-allowance); standard VAT accounting or the flat rate scheme, chosen in advance (vat-regs-frs, hmrc-v-burke).

Timing genuine transactions: buying kit that is actually needed before or after 5 April; paying pension contributions or Gift Aid in the year where they give most relief; the Gift Aid carry-back election; choosing which year a trading loss is relieved; accelerating transition profit into a low-income year (fa2004-ss188-192-pensions, ita-gift-aid, ita-s64, fa2022-sch1-transition).

Claiming reliefs and allowances for the purpose Parliament intended: AIA, FYAs and the 100% zero-emission car FYA on real purchases; pension relief; Marriage Allowance; loss reliefs; voluntary Class 2 in a low-profit year (caa-s51a-aia, caa-cars, ita-marriage-allowance, nicra2023-s3-class2, gaar-guidance-2021 C5.6.2).
Reducing payments on account on a reasoned, documented estimate (tma-s59a-poa).

Correcting the past lawfully: amending a return within 12 months, overpayment relief within 4 years, voluntary disclosure of errors to cut penalties, and asking for unclaimed reliefs in any late assessment (tma-s9za, tma-s43-sch1ab, fa2007-sch24, tma-s36).
Disclosing contestable positions in the return's white space to get finality, and holding HMRC to proof of discovery and time-limit conditions (langham-v-veltema, burgess-brimheath, hmrc-v-harte).
Appealing penalties and decisions on statutory grounds, with evidence of reasonable excuse, within the 30-day window (perrin-v-hmrc, tma-ss31-31a-49).

Getting employment status right engagement by engagement, keeping evidence of self-employment factors, and asking HMRC's Film and Production Unit to confirm status (hall-v-lorimer, hmrc-v-pgmol-uksc, esm4120, esm4104-4110).
Using statutory exit routes for past schemes, such as the 2026 Loan Charge Settlement Scheme (fa2026-ss25-27-loan-settlement).
refuse: Hiding or not declaring income, including cash jobs, uninvoiced PO work or receipts into another person's account: this is evasion and can be the crime of cheating the public revenue (theft-act-1968-s32, r-v-mavji, dosanjh-v-r, tma-s106a-vata-s72).

Creating, altering, backdating or inflating receipts, invoices, mileage logs, call sheets or hotel folios, or describing private costs (holidays, everyday clothes, ordinary meals, commuting, family visits) as business costs (hmrc-criminal-investigation-policy, fa2007-sch24).

Taking freelance or contract pay as loans, advances, annuities, grants, trust payments or other 'non-taxable' payments, including non-compliant umbrella 'enhanced take-home' offers and contractor loan schemes (rangers-rfc-2012, ittoia-ss23a-23h-loan-charge, spotlight-60, spotlight-71, gaar-panel-2018-mr-n).

Recommending or helping with any arrangement that has a DOTAS scheme reference number, matches an HMRC Spotlight, or has no realistic prospect of the tax result claimed (fa2004-dotas, spotlights-collection, fa2026-promoters).
Circular finance, inflated prices or 'investment' schemes designed to generate capital allowances or losses greater than the money really spent (tower-mcashback, seven-individuals).

Inserting artificial steps, entities, offshore companies, LLP memberships or third-party 'lenders' whose only purpose is a tax result (furniss-v-dawson, irc-v-mcguckian, rossendale-hurstwood, fa2013-gaar).
Setting up a company purely to escape employment status or PAYE on engagements that are really employment (esm4104-4110).
Splitting invoices or a business dishonestly to stay below the VAT registration threshold (tma-s106a-vata-s72, vata-sch1-threshold).
Schemes claiming to avoid or settle the loan charge outside HMRC's statutory routes, such as deeds of release or asset transfers (spotlights-collection, loan-charge-guidance-2026).
Helping the user help anyone else (a client, colleague or supplier) to evade tax (tma-s106a-vata-s72, cfa2017-s45, fno2a2017-sch16-enablers).

Presenting non-deductible items as deductible, such as fines, penalties, settlements in place of penalties, client entertainment or interest on late tax (scottishpower-v-hmrc, mcknight-v-sheppard, ittoia-s45).
Inventing or misquoting authorities, or claiming HMRC 'approval' for any arrangement (hmrc-v-gunnarsson, named-schemes).
planning_boundary.explanation: Everyone may arrange genuine affairs so as to pay less tax: in duke-of-westminster Lord Tomlin said every man is entitled, if he can, to order his affairs so that the tax under the Acts is less than it otherwise would be. Since ramsay, furniss-v-dawson and irc-v-mcguckian, however, the courts no longer let that principle protect artificial schemes. bmbf-v-mawson and rossendale-hurstwood state the modern test: read the statute purposively and ask whether it was meant to apply to the transaction viewed realistically, so pre-planned, circular or inserted steps whose only purpose is tax are disregarded, and allowances follow only real spending (tower-mcashback). irc-v-willoughby and the official definitions in hmt-tackling-avoidance-2019 draw the line Expend uses: tax planning or mitigation means using reliefs for the purpose Parliament intended and genuinely bearing their economic consequences; avoidance means bending the rules to get an advantage Parliament never intended; evasion is always illegal. The General Anti-Abuse Rule (fa2013-gaar, with a 60% penalty under fa2013-s212a) counteracts arrangements that cannot reasonably be regarded as a reasonable course of action, but HMRC's own approved GAAR guidance (gaar-guidance-2021) confirms that choosing between statutory options and claiming reliefs such as capital allowances and pensions is not abusive. rangers-rfc-2012 shows that earnings routed through a trust or a 'loan' remain earnings; for a sole trader ittoia-ss23a-23h-loan-charge does the same for trade income, and hoey-v-hmrc shows the worker bears the tax if the scheme fails. At the far end, hiding income or falsifying records is criminal (theft-act-1968-s32, tma-s106a-vata-s72, r-v-mavji, dosanjh-v-r), and promoting hopeless schemes is now an offence (fa2026-promoters). So Expend helps with real expenses, statutory method choices, timing of real transactions and reliefs used as intended, and refuses anything artificial, concealed or untrue, pointing the user instead to lawful routes such as disclosure, amendment and HMRC's settlement schemes.

savings_checklist.title: Choose the best method for your own car or van: fixed mileage rate or actual costs plus capital allowances
savings_checklist.legal_basis: ittoia-ss94d-94g, teva-2026-s2, caa-s1a, caa-cars, fa2026-s28-wda, bim75005, bim37007
savings_checklist.conditions: Own car, van or motorcycle used for deductible business journeys (not ordinary commuting). The choice is made per vehicle at its first claim and is locked while that vehicle is used in the trade. Mileage is barred if capital allowances were ever claimed on the vehicle, or if a van or motorcycle's cost was deducted on the cash basis.
savings_checklist.data_needed: mileage trips, expenses by category, equipment purchases, profit
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Mileage method: business miles in each tax year x 45p (2023-24 to 2025-26) or 55p (2026-27) for the first 10,000, then 25p; motorcycles 24p; add parking, tolls and congestion charges for business journeys. Actual method: (fuel + insurance + road tax + MOT + servicing + repairs + finance interest) x business-mileage share, plus capital allowances on the vehicle (main pool 18% to 2025-26 and 14% for 2026-27 for cars up to 50g/km, special-rate 6% otherwise, or 100% FYA for a new zero-emission car bought by 5 April 2027), reduced for private use. Compare over the expected ownership period, not just one year. Saving = extra deduction x (marginal income tax rate + Class 4 rate).
savings_checklist.risks: Irreversible for that vehicle. Needs a contemporaneous log (date, from, to, purpose, miles, job link). Trips to a regular venue or depot are commuting (samadian-v-hmrc, jackman-v-powell, noel-white-v-hmrc). Private detours taint a journey. Never claim both methods for one vehicle. Selling a car on which allowances were claimed creates a balancing adjustment.

savings_checklist.title: Claim travel from home to temporary venues and between venues
savings_checklist.legal_basis: ittoia-ss5-34, horton-v-young, samadian-v-hmrc, bim37600-37635, bim37670-37675-37677, newsom-v-robertson, jackman-v-powell, noel-white-v-hmrc, mellor-v-hmrc
savings_checklist.conditions: The trade is genuinely itinerant: many different, unpredictable venues, with home as the real business base (bookings, quotes, admin, kit). Not available for a venue, studio, warehouse or depot attended on a regular, predictable pattern, or where home is outside the area in which the work is done.
savings_checklist.data_needed: mileage trips, job days, stays, expenses by category
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Sum trains, coaches, flights, taxis, ferries and (if the mileage rate is not used for that vehicle) fuel for journeys linked to jobs. Flag for review any venue attended on many days in a year, or making up a large share of the year's job days, as a possible regular place of business.
savings_checklist.risks: A long engagement or recurring venue can become a place of business, ending travel, hotel and meal deductions for it. A trip combined with a holiday fails entirely (BIM37610). Each journey needs evidence: job reference, PO or call sheet.

savings_checklist.title: Deduct hire cars for gigs and tours in full
savings_checklist.conditions: Car hired for business journeys. On the cash basis no 15% restriction applies at all. On the accruals basis the 15% cut applies only to cars over 50g/km hired for more than 45 consecutive days (linked hires with gaps of 14 days or less count together).
savings_checklist.data_needed: expenses by category, job days, mileage trips
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Hire charge + fuel + business-use insurance or excess cover, less any private days. For long accruals-basis hires of non-low-emission cars, deduct 85% of the hire charge.
savings_checklist.risks: Exclude private days. Hire-car miles are not mileage-rate miles. Hires arranged mainly to avoid the 45-day rule lose the exception.

savings_checklist.title: Claim hotels and overnight subsistence on away jobs (including the night before an early call)
savings_checklist.legal_basis: bim47700-47705, bim37670-37675-37677, hmrc-v-healy-ut, healy-v-hmrc-ftt-2015, sean-reed-v-hmrc, hamish-taylor-v-hmrc, hanlin-v-hmrc, watkis-v-ashford-sparkes, maasher-v-hmrc
savings_checklist.conditions: The job makes a night away from home necessary (distance, early call, late finish); travel to the venue is itself deductible; the accommodation is not at a base of operations; and its only purpose is business (no family or friends staying, no bigger place chosen to host them).
savings_checklist.data_needed: stays, job days, mileage trips, expenses by category
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Hotel or short-let cost for business nights, plus a reasonable evening meal and breakfast; strip out private nights as an identifiable part (s34(2)). For long single-location runs, check the Healy factors: contract term, going home at weekends, not moving belongings in.
savings_checklist.risks: Long stays in one place covering several jobs can become a base (hamish-taylor-v-hmrc, hanlin-v-hmrc, prior-v-saunders). Dual-purpose accommodation fails entirely (healy-v-hmrc-ftt-2015). Record the business reason: call sheet or PO, distance, travel time.

savings_checklist.title: Claim reasonable meals while travelling to temporary venues
savings_checklist.conditions: Travel to the place is deductible, and either the trade is itinerant or the trip is occasional and outside the normal pattern of travel. Not for lunches at a regular or local venue.
savings_checklist.data_needed: job days, mileage trips, expenses by category
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Sum food and drink receipts dated on qualifying travel or job days at temporary venues, keeping each day's total at a reasonable level.
savings_checklist.risks: Regular local meals are not deductible (caillebotte-v-quinn). Buying for clients or crew is entertainment and barred (ittoia-s45).

savings_checklist.title: Get relief for equipment in the right year (cash-basis expensing or AIA)
savings_checklist.legal_basis: ittoia-s33a, ittoia-s24a, caa-s51a-aia, caa-s38b-s12-s13, fa2026-s29-fya, fa2026-s28-wda, ittoia-s96a, bim35901-35415, bmbf-v-mawson, tower-mcashback
savings_checklist.conditions: Kit bought for continuing use in the trade. On the cash basis (the default from 2024-25) it is deductible when paid, except cars, land, non-depreciating assets, training and the other s33A exclusions. On the accruals basis, AIA up to £1m (not for cars, not in the year the trade ceases), and a partial AIA claim is allowed.
savings_checklist.data_needed: equipment purchases, profit
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Cash basis: deduct the business share of each purchase in the tax year it was paid. Accruals: claim AIA, choosing the amount so profit stays just above the personal allowance or basic-rate band where that saves more, and leave the rest for WDAs (18% to 2025-26, 14% for 2026-27). For timing, compare buying before or after 5 April using each year's marginal rates. Short-life consumables are revenue on either basis.
savings_checklist.risks: Selling expensed kit, insurance pay-outs and moving kit to private use create taxable receipts (ittoia-s96a). Exclude any private-use share. Kit brought in from private ownership gets WDAs at market value, not AIA. The 50% FYA and 12% WDA from 2027 are proposed, not law. Circular or inflated-price kit schemes fail (tower-mcashback).

savings_checklist.title: Review cash basis against accruals (GAAP) each year
savings_checklist.conditions: A non-excluded trade (a freelance technician is not excluded). The election is made on the SA return and continues until revoked; switching creates adjustments.
savings_checklist.data_needed: profit, expenses by category, equipment purchases
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Cash: receipts banked in the tax year minus expenses paid. Accruals: invoices for work done in the year (including unpaid ones) minus expenses incurred, with capital allowances and bad-debt relief. Compare the tax over two or three years, including the switching adjustment. Cash usually wins where clients pay late or kit spending is high.
savings_checklist.risks: Switching adjustments can bring income forward. The election sticks until revoked. For 2023-24 the old cash basis had a £150,000 entry limit, a £500 interest cap and no sideways loss relief.

savings_checklist.title: Claim use of home: flat rate or actual costs, whichever is higher
savings_checklist.conditions: For the flat rate, at least 25 hours a month working at home wholly and exclusively on the business. Actual costs need a reasonable apportionment by area and time, and fixed costs only for space set aside solely for the business.
savings_checklist.data_needed: home working, expenses by category, phone and broadband
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Flat rate: for each month, £10 (25-50 hours), £18 (51-100) or £26 (101 or more). Actual: running costs (heat, light, power, cleaning) x business room-area share x business-hours share, plus fixed costs (council tax, insurance, mortgage interest, rent) for space used solely for business. Take the higher. The business share of phone and broadband goes on top either way.
savings_checklist.risks: Exclusive business use of a room may affect CGT private residence relief on a sale. Keep a log of home hours. On 2023-24 cash-basis profits the £500 interest cap applied.

savings_checklist.title: Claim the business share of phone and broadband
savings_checklist.conditions: Identifiable business use. The full cost is allowable where private use is not significant.
savings_checklist.data_needed: phone and broadband, expenses by category
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Work out the business share from a representative sample of itemised bills (calls, data) and apply it to the line rental, contract and broadband costs.
savings_checklist.risks: Keep the sample-period evidence and review the percentage if use changes.

savings_checklist.title: Claim protective clothing, PPE and branded uniform, but not everyday clothes
savings_checklist.conditions: Covers safety boots, gloves, hard hats, hi-vis, fall-arrest kit and branded crew uniform. Plain blacks and other ordinary clothing do not qualify.
savings_checklist.data_needed: expenses by category
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Sum PPE and uniform purchases. Exclude ordinary clothing even if worn only for work.
savings_checklist.risks: Plain show blacks fail under mallalieu-v-drummond.

savings_checklist.title: Claim training that updates or extends skills in your existing field
savings_checklist.conditions: Covers refreshers, certification renewals (IPAF, PASMA, rigging, first aid) and training on a new console or software. Retraining for an unrelated career does not qualify.
savings_checklist.data_needed: expenses by category
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Course fees, plus travel and accommodation for a deductible course.
savings_checklist.risks: A course giving a new qualification for a new area of work is capital, and on the cash basis s33A bars it.

savings_checklist.title: Deduct business interest and finance costs in full (2024-25 onward)
savings_checklist.conditions: Interest and finance charges on business borrowing (van, kit, business card). From 2024-25 the cash basis has no £500 cap.
savings_checklist.data_needed: expenses by category, equipment purchases
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Interest and finance charges for the period, less any private element. On the cash basis for 2023-24 the deduction was limited to £500.
savings_checklist.risks: Capital repayments are not deductible. Interest on late tax (ITTOIA s54) and penalties are never deductible.

savings_checklist.title: Make personal pension contributions to save higher-rate tax
savings_checklist.conditions: Relevant UK earnings must at least equal the gross contribution, or the contribution is limited to £3,600 gross. It must fit within the annual allowance (£60,000, plus carry-forward from the 3 previous years if a scheme member then). It counts in the tax year it is paid.
savings_checklist.data_needed: profit, other income (ask), pension contributions (ask)
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Gross contribution = net paid / 0.8. Higher-rate saving = 20% of the gross amount that falls within the higher-rate band (because the basic-rate band is extended). Between £100,000 and £125,140 of adjusted net income, each £1 gross also restores 50p of personal allowance (about 60% effective relief). There is no Class 4 saving.
savings_checklist.risks: Funds are locked until pension age. An annual allowance charge applies if the allowance is exceeded. The money purchase annual allowance (£10,000) applies if pensions were already flexibly accessed. Check scheme membership in the carry-forward years.

savings_checklist.title: Restore the personal allowance, and reduce the High Income Child Benefit Charge, with pension contributions or Gift Aid
savings_checklist.conditions: Adjusted net income over £100,000 (personal allowance taper), or over £60,000 where the user or a partner claims Child Benefit (ask).
savings_checklist.data_needed: profit, other income (ask), pension contributions (ask)
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Adjusted net income = net income - gross Gift Aid - gross relief-at-source pension contributions. Allowance lost = 50% of the excess over £100,000. HICBC = 1% of the Child Benefit for each £200 over £60,000, the full amount at £80,000. Model the gross contribution that brings adjusted net income down to £100,000 or £60,000.
savings_checklist.risks: Needs accurate figures for other income. HICBC can be collected by discovery assessment (hmrc-v-wilkes is superseded by FA 2022 s97).

savings_checklist.title: Use Gift Aid band extension and the carry-back election
savings_checklist.conditions: Donations to charity with a Gift Aid declaration (ask about donations), and enough tax paid to cover the basic-rate tax treated as deducted. The carry-back election must be made by the date the previous year's return is filed, and no later than its 31 January deadline.
savings_checklist.data_needed: profit, other income (ask)
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Gross gift = net / 0.8. Higher-rate relief = 20% (25% at the additional rate) of the gross amount falling in the higher bands. Compare the current year with the previous year to decide on carry-back.
savings_checklist.risks: The shortfall is clawed back if too little tax was paid (s424).

savings_checklist.title: Claim Marriage Allowance where one partner has income under £12,570
savings_checklist.conditions: Married or in a civil partnership. The recipient is a basic-rate taxpayer and the transferor's income is below the personal allowance. Claims can be backdated to 2022-23.
savings_checklist.data_needed: marital status (ask), profit, other income (ask)
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Up to £252 a year (20% of £1,260), plus any backdated years.
savings_checklist.risks: Not available if the recipient pays tax at the higher rate. The transferor gives up £1,260 of their allowance.

savings_checklist.title: Use trading losses in the most valuable year
savings_checklist.legal_basis: ita-s64, ita-s66, ita-ss72-74, ita-s83, ita-s24a-cap, ita-ss89-91, fa2024-sch10, seven-individuals, beacon-v-hmrc, macdonald-v-hmrc
savings_checklist.conditions: The trade is run commercially with a view to profit. Claims are due by the first anniversary of the 31 January filing date for the loss year (a 2024-25 loss by 31 January 2027). Cash-basis losses for 2023-24 could not be set sideways.
savings_checklist.data_needed: profit, other income (ask), equipment purchases
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Compare the tax saved by setting the loss against: this year's total income; the previous year's; the three years before the loss under early-years carry-back (first four tax years of the trade); or future profits by carry-forward. Allow for wasted personal allowance and the s24A cap (the greater of £50,000 and 25% of adjusted total income).
savings_checklist.risks: Repeated losses invite a s66 commerciality challenge. Sideways relief can waste the personal allowance. The deadlines are strict.

savings_checklist.title: Reduce payments on account when profits fall
savings_checklist.conditions: A reasoned expectation that this year's liability will be lower than last year's. Claim by 31 January after the tax year, online or on SA303.
savings_checklist.data_needed: payments on account, profit, pension contributions (ask), other income (ask)
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Reduced payment on account = (estimated income tax + Class 4 for the current year, less tax deducted at source) / 2. Compare with each payment due. The cash saved is held until the balancing payment.
savings_checklist.risks: Interest at Bank Rate + 4% (8.00% from 24 November 2026) on any shortfall. A fraudulent or negligent claim can bring a penalty up to the shortfall (s59A(6)).

savings_checklist.title: Recover missed expenses before the deadlines
savings_checklist.conditions: Amend the return within 12 months of the filing date (2024-25 until 31 January 2027). Otherwise claim overpayment relief within 4 years of the tax year end (2022-23 until 5 April 2027), subject to the Sch 1AB exclusions. A missed capital allowance claim generally needs an amendment instead.
savings_checklist.data_needed: expenses by category, equipment purchases, profit
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Find ledger items categorised as deductible that were left out of the filed return. Saving = extra deduction x marginal rate (income tax + Class 4).
savings_checklist.risks: Reasonable excuse does not extend these deadlines (hmrc-v-raftopoulou). An amendment opens an enquiry window into the amendment.

savings_checklist.title: Bring basis-period transition profit forward into a low-income year
savings_checklist.conditions: Applies only if the accounting date before 2024-25 was not 31 March to 5 April. The election deadline is the first anniversary of the year's filing date: 2024-25 by 31 January 2027, 2025-26 by 31 January 2028, 2026-27 by 31 January 2029.
savings_checklist.data_needed: profit, other income (ask)
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Tax on transition profit = tax with it minus tax without it (notional calculation). Compare bringing an extra slice into a year with spare personal allowance or basic-rate band against the default 20% a year to 2026-27, with the balance in 2027-28.
savings_checklist.risks: Overlap relief was usable only in 2023-24. The notional calculation can reduce the personal allowance above £100,000.

savings_checklist.title: Protect your state pension cheaply in a low-profit year
savings_checklist.conditions: Profits below the small profits threshold (£6,725 for 2024-25, £6,845 for 2025-26, £7,105 for 2026-27) while UK-based.
savings_checklist.data_needed: profit
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Voluntary Class 2 costs the weekly rate (£3.45, £3.50 or £3.65) x 52, about £180-£190 a year, against Class 3 at £17.45, £17.75 or £18.40 a week.
savings_checklist.risks: Check the National Insurance record first. From 2026-27, voluntary Class 2 cannot be paid for periods abroad.

savings_checklist.title: Compare the trading allowance with actual expenses for side income
savings_checklist.conditions: Small additional trading or miscellaneous income, not paid by the user's own employer, partnership or close company.
savings_checklist.data_needed: expenses by category, profit, other income (ask)
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Deduct the greater of actual expenses and £1,000 (£3,000 from 2027-28 if enacted). For the main freelance trade, actual expenses almost always win.
savings_checklist.risks: The allowance is one figure shared across all trading and miscellaneous income. £3,000 is proposed, not law.

savings_checklist.title: Monitor the VAT threshold and model voluntary registration and the flat rate scheme
savings_checklist.conditions: Rolling 12-month taxable turnover near £90,000 (registration compulsory above it) or below it (registration voluntary). Clients are mostly VAT-registered production companies.
savings_checklist.data_needed: profit, expenses by category, equipment purchases
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Total invoiced turnover from the ledger for the rolling 12 months at each month-end. Benefit of voluntary registration = input VAT on kit, hire, hotels and fuel (from receipts showing VAT) minus admin cost, provided clients can recover the VAT charged. For the flat rate scheme, compare 16.5% (limited cost trader) or the sector rate x VAT-inclusive turnover with output VAT minus input VAT.
savings_checklist.risks: Missing the threshold brings late-registration penalties and backdated VAT. The FRS is usually poor value for labour-heavy trades. There is no retrospective FRS switching (hmrc-v-burke). Choose a reasonable sector and record why (jjk-engineering).

savings_checklist.title: Time a new zero-emission car purchase for the 100% FYA (by 5 April 2027)
savings_checklist.conditions: A new, unused electric or 0g/km car bought by 5 April 2027 (income tax) for business use, claimed through capital allowances rather than the mileage rate.
savings_checklist.data_needed: equipment purchases, mileage trips
savings_checklist.how_to_estimate: Allowance = cost x 100% x business-use share in the year of purchase. Compare with the mileage rate at 55p/25p over the expected ownership period.
savings_checklist.risks: The allowance is restricted for private use. A balancing charge arises on sale. Choosing allowances rules out the mileage rate for that car.

savings_checklist.title: Avoid late-filing and late-payment penalties and interest, and estimate any that are due
savings_checklist.legal_basis: tma-s8, fa2009-sch55, fa2009-sch56, fa2021-ss116-118, si-2026-370, si-2025-589, govuk-mtd-penalties, penalty-reform-all-sa-2027, si-2025-386-interest, govuk-hmrc-interest-rates, perrin-v-hmrc, donaldson-v-hmrc, barry-edwards-v-hmrc, harrison-v-hmrc, tma-ss31-31a-49, fa2026-ss259-264
